speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF ADDITIONAL SALE TO POLAND
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, further to my announcement on June 6 concerning the sale of wheat to Poland, I should like now to inform the house that an additional contract for 100,000 tons of wheat has been signed between the Canadian wheat board and the Polish national trade organization Rolimpex.
The government has authorized export credits insurance to facilitate this sale, the terms being the same as in the first agreement. Shipment of this wheat is to take place during the current crop year. This contract brings the total amount of wheat sold to Poland this year to 7.5 million bushels.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question
to the Prime Minister and ask him if he has seen the editorial appearing in this morning's Globe and Mail entitled "A Knife for Mr. Gordon", which concludes with the following sentence:
If the government wants to remove Mr. Gordon it should do so openly, accept the full responsibility, and give the public its reasons. To use backbenchers to do the dirty work is unworthy of national leaders.
Has the Prime Minister any comment to make on this editorial?
Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime
Minister): Mr. Speaker, I have always followed the course of not making comments on editorials, and this occasion will be no exception.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Does the Prime Minister not think that this is a disgraceful manner in which to proceed-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: Order. It seems to me that the question is argumentative, to say the least.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: Well, Mr. Speaker, I feel that I have the right to ask a supplementary question.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: Yes, but may I suggest to the hon. member that I was doubtful as to the propriety of his first question, and the hon. gentleman's second question is certainly out of order because it is argumentative.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. May I point out to Your Honour, in the first place, that with all respect to what you have said I think it is quite in order to ask the Prime Minister a question based on an editorial. Your Honour saw fit to allow the question. The supplementary question was not going to proceed on that basis. I now propose to ask Your Honour if I am not in order in asking the Prime Minister whether it is the practice to use backbenchers to do the work which the government should do.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT

speechtext:

speak to the point of order, Mr. Speaker, I believe it is correct to say that questions based on editorials are not in order. It is not in order to refer to editorial comment in the house. I would submit with great deference, however, that it is in order to ask the government about an important question of policy relating to the government's attitude toward the appointment of the president of the Canadian National Railways or his continuation in office. I think it is very pertinent, because the question has been raised on frequent occasions and there has been much public comment and speculation.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: Order. I have not ruled that all questions pertaining to the appointment of the president of the Canadian National Railways would be out of order. I have merely indicated that the questions put by the hon. member for Laurier were, in my view, clearly out of order. If the hon. member for Assiniboia has a question to put on the subject he may proceed to do so, but I suggest that discussing the point of order in order to emphasize or underline an argument would not be a regular course to follow.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT
speechtext: May I then ask the government if it will announce at an early date its policy toward the president of the Canadian National Railways, and whether his term of service will be extended for a particular period.

subtopic: GOVERNMENT POLICY RESPECTING APPOINTMENT OF PRESIDENT

They have gone through the estimates of the Department of Transport as meticulously and carefully as the opposition are capable of within their limitations. Having done that, I am sure the committee will meet at the earliest possible date, and that the desire for discussion and consideration of the report will be entirely met.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I wish to direct a question of more urgency to the Minister of National Defence. Will the minister outline how the federal government is answering the request received from the province of Saskatchewan for assistance in the battle against the grasshoppers now threatening the western crops?

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minister of National Defence):
speakerposition: Minister of National Defence
subtopic: SASKATCHEWAN
subsubtopic: R.C.A.F. ASSISTANCE IN COMBATING GRASSHOPPERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Thursday evening I received an urgent request from the Saskatchewan minister of agriculture for assistance in getting grasshopper poison out .to Saskatchewan, as they had run short of it. In response to this request I authorized the Royal Canadian Air Force to assist in combating the infestation in Saskatchewan by airlifting the badly needed supply of insecticides from Toronto to Regina. This emergency airlift commenced on Friday, June 9, in the afternoon and will continue until an adequate supply of insecticide is available to overcome


the threat. It is anticipated that the airlift necessary to do this will be completed some time today.

subtopic: SASKATCHEWAN

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, yesterday I had just commenced answering the general inquiries that had been made on this first item and I had not quite completed my remarks. As a matter of courtesy to those hon. members-

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order. I am having some difficulty hearing the minister. I wonder whether we could have quiet in the committee, please.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
As a matter of courtesy to those hon. members who made comments or suggestions I think I should complete my reply. In connection with the remarks of the hon. member for Kootenay West on the standards of training and qualifications of members of the security and intelligence branch, and dealing specifically with the comments as to language training, I might say that we have a number of personnel in that division who are well qualified indeed so far as a knowledge of foreign languages is concerned. At any time that we required further training from this point of view we would not hesitate to send our personnel on the necessary courses.
I might also point out that in addition to actual academic training we have in our force constables and N.C.O.'s from every ethnic group in Canada with the exception of the Eskimo group, and we are now trying to get a qualified Eskimo who might be available to join the force. I should point out that at the present time we have a number of special constables in the force who are Eskimos. Let me emphasize again that we have members and N.C.O.'s from every other ethnic group in Canada.
It might interest hon. members if I were to put on the record a list of the ethnic and language groups from which our members are drawn and the totals in each group. In the totals I show here I would emphasize that these members speak fluently the language in question: German, 169; Ukrainian, 202; Russian, 46; Polish, 70; Czech, 18; Hungarian, 12; Yugoslav, 7; Bulgarian, 1; Rumanian, 2; Croatian 1; Slovakian, 5; Latvian, 1; Lithuanian, 5; Greek, 2; Italian, 24; Spanish, 3; Dutch, 22; Flemish, 2; Yiddish, 4; Swedish 13; Norwegian, 21; Danish, 15; Icelandic, 14; Finnish, 4; Japanese 2; Chinese, 2; Eskimo, 1; Cree, 1; Gaelic, 5; Swahili, the language used in the Congo and Kenya, 2; Arabic 1. In so far as Eskimo is concerned, I point out that we have one member who speaks this language fluently, although he is not himself an

Eskimo, and we have a number who have a knowledge of the language, but we would not qualify them as fluent.
The hon. member for Maisonneuve-Rose-mont raised a question with regard to dog teams in the territories. I can assure him that it is not the normal practice to fly dog teams around the territories. Such circumstances would only arise very rarely. Normally the patrols would be undertaken from the detachment where the dog teams are kept. It would only be if the incident which required investigation took place in a very remote area that the dog teams would be flown to another point from which the patrol by dog team would actually start. We have, in fact, eight snowmobiles stationed at various points throughout the territories. Some years ago we did make an experiment with an auto-toboggan. The one with which the experiment was then conducted was found not to be suitable.
Now, with regard to the question concerning the increase in the number of dogs, I think the hon. member has misconstrued the circumstances. We are not undertaking an overall increase, certainly no substantial increase in the number of dogs. There is a program under way, however, for breeding a new type of husky, a Siberian husky, which research has shown to be more amenable, more easily trained and a less dangerous animal than the present type of sled dog in use throughout the territories. There have been some very unpleasant attacks upon persons by sled dogs, not so much by our dogs-because I think we have them under pretty good control at all times-but these attacks on humans have been made by the type of husky which has been in use up there. We believe we should first establish the use of the new type dogs ourselves, and then encourage their use throughout the whole of the territories.
The hon. member for Chapleau raised the very difficult problem of the enforcement of the pleasure boat regulations. This is a work that is of increasing concern and difficulty to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. At the moment there are an estimated three quarters of a million pleasure boats in Canada, and this total is rising rapidly. The problem of enforcement of the small boat regulations is becoming acute, and one which requires a great deal of planning. We are concerned lest our planning and the recruiting of our establishment cannot keep pace with the increasing demands that are made upon us.
In this connection I might point out that our difficulty in this is a summertime problem. It is difficult indeed, as hon. members will understand, to persuade treasury board that we should be allowed the increase in our establishment necessary to take care of the volume of work which this entails in the
Supply-R.C.M.P.
summer, because if that were done then there would be the problem of whether or not we had more men than we needed at other times. We have not really been able to get any special establishment for this work. I may point out that with the limited establishment we have now we made 41,000 separate checks last year, and the information collected in these investigations resulted in 607 convictions.
We do feel that this is a problem for which the public of Canada should not expect the sole responsibility to be assumed by the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The use of motorboats and pleasure boats has reached a point where it may well be equated with the use of motor vehicles on the highway. Instead of driving cars for pleasure or touring, people frequently drive their boats or there is a combination of the two, the boats being towed on trailers behind the cars and put in the lakes and then the boats are used for tourism. Just as the Royal Canadian Mounted Police could hardly be thought, indeed is not thought, to be responsible for checking the extra summer traffic on the highways, it is our view that we should not be held exclusively responsible for checking the extra summer traffic on our waterways which is brought about by the influx of tourists.
We feel quite strongly it is only proper that we should suggest the provinces, and indeed the municipalities, might assume extra responsibility in this direction. I think hon. members will be interested to know that some of the regulations with regard to small boats are to be moved out of the regulations under the Canada Shipping Act and incorporated in amendments to the Criminal Code which I will be introducing later. We feel this is quite proper because not only is the traffic in small boats assuming such proportions that the provisions regarding safe driving should really become part of the criminal law, but this will have the additional result that, being part of the criminal law, it will no longer be the sole responsibility of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police to enforce these laws.
The hon. member for Hull raised questions about bilingual personnel on parliament hill. In view of the number of persons who come from all over Canada and, naturally, from the province of Quebec, to visit the hill, it is most desirable that we should have bilingual personnel here. I must say that we agree entirely with the hon. gentleman, and follow this policy within the limits of the resources at our disposal in having bilingual personnel stationed on parliament hill, especially during the summer months.

Supply-R.C.M.P.
Will any statement be made on the question of the Chinese immigration inquiry which I raised yesterday?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I think the proper approach to this problem is that policy statements with respect to the Chinese immigration inquiry should be made by my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration. I think I should go no further at this point than to say that when the minister announced the inquiry and the steps that had been taken to date and would be taken in the subsequent period, she said that she counted particularly, in what is described colloquially but somewhat inaccurately as the amnesty program, on the co-operation of the Chinese community to clear those who might be referred to as innocent passengers in this traffic and to establish who are the ringleaders in organized criminal activity. Unfortunately we have not found that co-operation forthcoming to the extent that we had hoped and to the extent that I believe we were entitled to expect.
My friend the hon. member for Vancouver Centre, in speaking on the introduction of my estimates some two or three weeks ago, made a statement in this regard. As he is a Canadian of Chinese origin it came particularly appropriately from him. The hon. gentleman in his statement outlined his consideration and study of the matter, and expressed regret that the degree of co-operation that might have been expected had not been forthcoming.
I can only say that while we have had some prosecutions and have achieved some success in obtaining evidence that established clearly the culpability of some of those who are quite prominent in the racketeering that was going on, we have not made all the progress that we had hoped for and it may be some time before we can record substantial progress. The matter is causing a very great deal of concern, and it has been the subject of discussion between my colleague and myself from the point of view of whether or not the time has arrived-and there are many considerations that argue that it has- when perhaps a new approach, taking advantage of some of the other provisions of the law which so far we have not invoked, might be warranted.

Can the minister give a progress report on the R.C.M.P. investigation? A statement on the subject from the minister would give an assurance that I am certain would be welcomed by the Canadian Chinese community.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I have to say, with regret, that I am not in a position to

give an authoritative and final statement because, as I have indicated, we are unfortunately not receiving the co-operation which we expected and to which I think we are entitled, when one considers that one of the main objects of our inquiry is to clear up this situation once and for all and to establish and regularize the position of those Chinese who may be in Canada on the basis of irregular entry but with respect to whom, as my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration said, there is no intention of prosecuting or pushing out of Canada when they themselves were only innocent passengers in this traffic. I hope that in the course of the reasonable future we might be able to bring some finality to the matter and at that time one could make a statement, but at the present time because of the stone wall of refusal to give information which is clearly within the knowledge of those concerned we have not been able to make the progress we would like to have made.
As I said, this is a matter of concern and discussion between my colleague and myself as to whether we should invoke some of the other provisions of the law which are available but which so far we have not relied upon, in order to obtain this information that we must have in the interests of the Chinese community itself.
Mr. Chairman, I wish to speak about a matter-

Mr. Chairman, if the hon. gentleman is going to speak on another subject I wonder if he would permit me to ask one question on the matter the minister has discussed. I should like to be assured by the minister that the government has no thought of receding from the solemn assurance given in this house by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration to the Chinese community at the last session of parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well, Mr. Chairman, there has been no change. Any change would have to be announced by my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration.
The question I ask is whether the government is contemplating withdrawing the assurance that was given.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not know to what assurance my hon. friend refers. There were several aspects to the assurance, as I recall it, and I am not in a position to make a categorical reply to that question.

I will recall the assurance for the assistance of the minister. The assurance, and it was a very precise one, was that no one would be deported from Canada merely because he had given information that

was not exact if he was in fact a relative of someone living in this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I do not recall the statement of my colleague sufficiently clearly to be certain that my hon. friend has accurately summarized it. The intent of my colleague's statement was to make clear that persons who with respect to themselves or their immediate relatives may have given misinformation in order to bring themselves or their relatives here to Canada, not for the purpose of profit, would not be pushed around or prosecuted. I do, however, recall my colleague saying that in order to establish these and all the other facts it would be necessary for us to have the co-operation of these people and truthful statements from them. It is the lack of co-operation that concerns us at the present time.

I should not like to think, and I am sure the minister does not intend it to be thought, that he is seeking to secure co-operation by holding a kind of veiled threat over these people that the word of the government given in this house is going to be withdrawn.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the word of the government, of course, stands. My hon. friend knows perfectly well that when the government makes statements with respect to situations such as this, based on an assumption that co-operation will be forthcoming, it is entitled to review the situation from time to time and to state its position in accordance with the developments so long as that position is stated clearly.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to bring to the attention of the minister the matter of the enforcement of federal statutes as applied to harness racing. This sport is vigorously pursued, at least in the province of Nova Scotia, and at the present time the personnel of the nearby R.C.M.P. detachments who are specially trained are required to attend these races while they are in progress to enforce the statutes. This duty is in addition to their normal detachment duties. It can readily be seen that because races are often held on holidays and on other special occasions this imposes an additional burden, over and above normal duties, on a few constables.
I wonder whether the minister would look into the matter and see if the establishments of the nearby detachments could be increased so that the tour of duty of all personnel would be less onerous. I understand that these constables receive no extra remuneration for the additional hours they are required to serve.
Supply-R.C.M.P.
While I am on my feet may I also tell the minister that the R.C.M.P. are performing a splendid service in my area not only in law enforcement but also in the contribution they make in the various communities.

Mr. Chairman, I rise briefly to refer to a matter about which I spoke yesterday. Apparently radio and television reports created interest in the complaints made yesterday in this committee by one or two hon. members in respect to the activities of the security section of the R.C.M.P. My telephone has been ringing constantly this morning, and I have already had phone calls or visits from students at Ottawa universities. I listened very carefully to what they had to say, and these very fine young people were very concerned about things that were happening in their universities.
I was recently informed that a student at an Ottawa university was approached by a young R.C.M.P. constable and asked whether he or she knew of any students with communist leanings or radical tendencies. This student was asked to report on the activities of certain persons who were interested in the ban the bomb movement-I think that is the common term for it-and those who were interested in the activities of the C.C.F.-New Party club. Now, what do you think of that?
That is a logical conclusion.

One of those students who visited me was particularly concerned about this question and is a member of a well known Ottawa family that has lived here a long time. This constable, in a rather aggressive way, tried to persuade this student to act as an informer on fellow students. It was brought to the attention of the constable that there are members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police attending these universities, and he was asked "Why not use them?" His reply was to the effect, "Well, they are busy in other directions"; they wanted to get one of the students to do this. These students were asked to inform from time to time upon the activities of the persons in these groups to the constable in question. I am glad to say that they rejected this suggestion with scorn, because I think it is the wrong way to go about this sort of thing.
I rise again on their behalf to protest most vigorously these attempts to make informers, cads and stoolpigeons of our students in universities. I say this is the wrong way to go about it. It is not a proper thing to do, to ask a young student, regardless of the motive, to spy and inform on fellow students while going to university.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, my hon. friend has of course used a great many sensational words in his remarks, and I can only regret

Supply-R.C.M.P.
that the hon. member, who usually has such a high sense ol responsibility, should make these statements without giving me an opportunity to examine the matter to see whether there in any justification for what he says. These anonymous, unestablished, unidentified complaints which are blown up and puffed up in a sensational manner so often result in unfair criticism, and I am surprised that the hon. member should have made these remarks without any consultation with me or any effort to establish whether there was in fact any basis or justification for them.
I am not denying that there is concern, or may be concern, on the part of the members of the security and intelligence service of the R.C.M. Police about activities on university campuses. Nor can one deny that it is an avowed objective of communism to infiltrate universities. It is an avowed objective of Canadian communists to do exactly that. It is an avowed objective of Canadian communism to infiltrate a number of organizations whose purposes, though perfectly innocent and proper, they could subvert to their own ends if they were able to infiltrate them successfully and obtain control.
We would be negligent and open to criticism if we turned a blind eye to this situation and said "We are going to be embarrassed and criticized if we make any inquiries about this matter, so we had better let the activity carry on without any attempt to check it to see to what extent, if any, this infiltration has become effective and successful."
My hon. friend knows that although his party has itself openly disavowed the suggestion that there has been any infiltration of communism into it, there have been repeated attempts by the communists to identify themselves with the movement of which he is a member. We detest this, but it is a communist objective.
I am not in a position to do so, nor am I going to succumb to the temptation or persuasion to say that with respect to this, that or any other activity which we know the communists are attempting to infiltrate we will call our efforts off and cancel our inquiries simply because some people say, and say quite rightly, "This is an obviously innocent and desirable group of persons and it is wrong for you to be taking this interest in what goes on".
I said yesterday that we are not concerned about or suspicious of the motives or the genuine, conscientious purposes of the people who have formed these associations, or students generally at university. But when we know that communists, as a matter of policy, are attempting to infiltrate these associations, then it becomes the responsibility of the

security force to keep a check on them and to establish the extent to which that objective is being realized.
I am sorry it does not seem possible to make this sort of effort without giving rise to some criticism. I do not maintain that our men are perfect, that they will never make mistakes or perhaps ask the wrong questions; but I do ask that there should be some measure of understanding with respect to our security and intelligence efforts regarding communism in Canada. I ask for understanding of the task which is imposed upon our security forces.
Particularly I do suggest that where there may be a feeling on the part of any individual that an improper approach was made, or where word is received by members of parliament or others that improper approaches were made to them, these matters should be brought to my attention, because I am as anxious as anyone else that the work in this field, difficult enough as it is, should not be made more difficult by blunders. We are always anxious to improve our methods and do what we can to carry them out without offence to the public, but this responsibility is imposed upon us and we have to discharge it.

Mr. Chairman, the minister knows that I do not raise a question unless I am convinced there is some substance in it. I questioned these people very closely and took down their words very carefully. I am objecting to the wrong approach in this matter. Hon. members know that people do not like their names being used in matters of this kind, but I will go into this question further and see whether I can assist the minister to make certain there is a proper approach to this question.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I would appreciate that co-operation. I have never maintained and never will maintain that we do not make mistakes, and we are anxious to know where mistakes have been made so that we may profit by them.

Mr. Chairman, this may be a small matter to raise in this committee, but I think it affects the prestige and the respect which the R.C.M. Police have across this country. I refer to the fact that they are now acting as meter maids at Malton airport. As I understand it, it costs some $2,000 a year to train an R.C.M.P. constable. Surely we can find some men who are over 50 or 55 years of age, who cannot find employment in other fields, who could very well carry out the work of supervising parking, checking cars and so on, at this airport. Chief constables all over the country are trying to get out of having

their men check the parking and carry out the tagging of cars, because they lose the respect of the public. Yet here we have members of a force which is recognized as second to none in the world acting as meter maids at Malton airport. I think it is a mistake and I hope it will be rectified.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
In reply, Mr. Chairman, the situation is that at the request of the Department of Transport, and for very good reason in view of the increasing traffic through our airports, the R.C.M. Police within recent months have assumed responsibility for policing Department of Transport airports.
It is true that in the take-over period we have had to put a number of men on the airports to acquaint themselves with all the responsibilities that policing airports involve, and during this period it is true that a minimum number of these men are actually doing some of the traffic control and parking enforcement. Ultimately, however, the intention is to have simply one of our uniformed men in charge of that work and responsible for it. The work that my hon. friend has referred to, namely the actual checking of cars, putting tags on them and checking parking meters, will be carried out by the corps of commissionaires, with one of our uniformed men supervising that work as part of our responsibility for policing the airports of Canada. It is the intention that our men shall not continue to do this type of work, for the reason the hon. member has stated.
I understand there were older men doing this job but that they were let out when the R.C.M.P. took over. Are these men to be given back their jobs?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The intention is to have the corps of commissionaires made responsible for the physical work of checking the parking and parking meters.

I should like to comment briefly on a practice which was prevalent at one time but which is now not so common. I refer to the procedure in connection with the prosecution of cases before the inferior courts, where the cases are not of such magnitude as to justify the province in providing counsel.
What often happens in the more remote areas or in the area of a detachment where there are only one or two men is this. When a complaint is made there will be an investigation by the N.C.O. or by a constable. Subsequently the same man may well serve the summons, and when the case comes before the magistrate the same N.C.O. or the same constable will appear and act as counsel in 90205-6-388
Supply-R.C.M.P.
the sense that he examines witnesses for the crown and cross-examines witnesses for the defence.
That is all right, but what I think is wrong is the situation where, having done that, the same constable or N.C.O. goes into the witness box and gives evidence. As I say, I think that practice is not very common today;
I have noticed a considerable lessening of the number of cases in which that procedure occurs, and it may well be that instructions have gone out to this effect.
The minister, as a member of the legal profession, will bear with me when I say that when a member of the legal profession acting as counsel takes off his gown and steps into the box to give evidence, it must only be in extraordinary circumstances that he does so. Bearing in mind that it is in the inferior courts where the majority of the people of this country make their first contact with the administration of justice, I do not think the practice to which I have referred makes a good impression. I realize that it is not as prevalent as it was, but I hope instructions can be given so that it is eliminated altogether except when it is essential that the practice be followed.
Having said that, I should like to add a word of tribute. For the last 35 years I have been daily engaged in actions in which I have acted for the defence. I have fought the good fight against the R.C.M.P. in a great many cases, and I hope I shall continue to do so. I may say that in my own district we have a situation where one officer and I think 39 N.C.O.'s and other ranks are responsible for an area of 70,000 square miles containing 75,000 people. They carry on a great deal of work for the province, and they act as police for many of the smaller municipalities. When one relates the number of men employed to the population in the area and compares that number with the number of policemen required in the larger centres and the metropolitan areas, it is obvious that they are doing a tremendous job. I make this comment having in mind that my contacts with the R.CjM.P. have always been as counsel for the defence, and it cannot be said I am prejudiced.
Bearing in mind that the force does this good work, may I point out that the construction of improved highways through our country is leading to a situation where more men may be required for patrol. There have been a number of fatal accidents in the last two or three years and, unfortunately, this good road, this symbol of civilization, goes hand in hand with a great deal of slaughter of people in traffic accidents. I hope some consideration may be given to providing extra men

Supply-R.C.M.P.
where required for highway patrol duty on the new highways which are being built.
One final point. I have known many members of the force in the old days, and I know the pension conditions which prevail for members of the force who retired many years ago. I hope some consideration may be given to increasing those pensions, many of which were fixed in days when conditions differed a great deal, in order to bring them into line with the inflated costs of the present day.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The hon. member for Col-chester-Hants asked me about the enforcement of race track betting laws, and drew attention to the number of extra hours members of the force responsible for this work in his area have to put in. This is a constant problem as far as we are concerned, and I would appreciate the support of all hon. members in endeavouring to get sufficient personnel to solve it effectively. We find it is not always easy to get agreement to our requests for increases in establishments. This is a matter of which we are aware, however, and I am constantly trying to get sufficient personnel to enable us to do all the jobs which we have to do, efficiently and without placing an undue burden on our personnel. But the day that happens and we find ourselves with an adequate establishment to do everything we are called upon to do, I think we shall see ourselves translated to another world. In the meantime I shall do my best to obtain the establishment we need.
The question raised by the hon. member for Peace River regarding personnel being on occasion both prosecutors and witnesses is an important and difficult one. I can tell the hon. member without equivocation that this is never undertaken as a matter of policy. As far as the mounted police are concerned as a federal force, we are opposed to it.
However, in eight of the ten provinces we are acting as a force under contract to the province. Conditions vary from province to province, and the situation is that in some regions arrangements are not made for the services of crown prosecutors. As a result we find a situation where the police are responsible both for conducting the prosecution and for giving evidence. Every effort is made to avoid putting the officer conducting the case in the position of having to enter the witness box and give evidence in the same case, but every now and then, because of the problem of personnel, it may be that the constable who has to give evidence is

the only one available to conduct the case. It may be that his colleague has been required for other duty.
We do not like this situation. We are in constant communication with the provinces urging them to make crown prosecutors available so these circumstances shall not arise. In Manitoba we have a generally happy situation in this respect. In Saskatchewan the situation is not at all the same; it is not at all happy, because we have been unable to persuade the Saskatchewan government that they should provide crown prosecutors. In British Columbia the situation varies. There are detachments where occasionally the same member of the force has to give evidence and conduct the case. We try to avoid the situation whenever we can, and we shall continue to bring pressure on the provinces for their assistance in solving this difficulty by providing adequate numbers of crown prosecutors.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I wish to say something on this question of security. It seems to me that the minister has done just about what his department has done in this field. I have always been interested in this matter of security because I have felt that the activities of the department in this regard cover a multitude of sins. I feel that when we are discussing the department's activities regarding the communist threat, in one way or another, we must keep two or three things in mind. First, communism in Canada is not illegal. Second, anyone who does admit publicly that he is a communist obviously is not in a position to be a threat as a spy.
I think the department uses this communist threat as an excuse and cover up for a multitude of sins committed in relation to security rights of individuals. I think the attitude of many members of that force in dealing with this communist business is expressed quite well in an article which appeared in the Ottawa Journal of June 7, 1961 under the heading "Below the Hill". The subject matter of this article is similar to that raised in a question asked a few moments ago regarding members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on duty at airports. I should like to quote the article, which reads as follows:
Mrs. Nora McAuley, 1309 Woodside Drive, is the latest victim of that gobbledygook and high-handed officialese so prevalent at the new Uplands air terminal. Her husband was flying to the north country Monday so Mrs. McAuley and her three young children drove with him to the terminal to wave goodbye. As they stopped in front of the rotunda, a commissionaire told Mr. McAuley that he couldn't help his wife getting the children out of the car "because you can't park here." When explanations failed, Mr. McAuley, who had little

time to catch his plane, went to get the baggage weighed. His wife and the kids decided to drive away without saying goodbye.
But oh no. The commissionaire had by this time summoned a mountie who demanded to know what Mrs. McAuley was doing at the airport. She told him. Who was her husband, the mountie demanded. Her husband was her husband, said Mrs. McAuley. Let me see your driver's licence, demanded the mountie. More questions. Mrs. McAuley tried to explain that she was leaving anyway. More questions. At last she broke into tears.
"Oh, all right," said the law. "You can go now."
That describes the type of thing that happens in the security field, only it is much more serious. The minister explained yesterday the educational advantages which were being given to some members of the R.C.M. Police. I should be very surprised to find that many of these individuals involved in the political investigation field are qualified to make any assessment of any information obtained. I understand that spying is a very complicated business, and that there are only a few individuals who are efficient in detecting spying activities.
Much of this political security work is being carried out in universities and in the mining communities of northern Ontario. There are probably more special officers of the R.C.M.P. security section per capita in those areas than anywhere else. Those individuals are questioning people, many of whom reply that they are communists but who actually are no more communistic than the majority of the members of this House of Commons. These people are individuals who at one time were workers in organizations like the "Wobblies" who came in contact with individuals who suggested that anyone who joined a union or labour organization was a communist. Many of these people have belonged to these organizations for 30 or 40 years and have no objection to being called communists because they do not have the faintest notion of the political implications.
It seems to me if the department wishes to increase its strength in this field in order to become an overweighted monster, it can do so through the activities which are now taking place. I suggest that if we are so violently opposed to communism, we should outlaw it and attempt to eliminate it in this country. I do not believe we should be successful in that way, because this would create an increase in communism in this country.
I suggest that communism is absolutely no threat as a political philosophy at the present time, nor will it be a threat as long as Canadians have an opportunity to improve their standard of living and continue to enjoy the benefits they are now enjoying. I suggest that communism is a threat only in countries such as those in South America, 90205-6-388J
Supply-R.C.M.P.
where the people are oppressed and suffer conditions of poverty, and are not able to even hope to change their situation under the forms of government which now exist. I suggest those are the countries and conditions in which communism flourishes.
I have had some experience with communist organization, having been involved in the mining field for some years. At one time the workers were represented by an organization considered to be communistic. I personally joined another organization which fought with that other organization for a considerable length of time. We know that the people who are interested in promoting communism in unions follow a certain pattern. I suggest it is possible, after considerable study, to recognize the line which will be followed by those people, and to know in advance the changes which will be made. I suggest that these facts are well known to the officials of the minister's department.
Surely, therefore, it is not necessary to continue this type of activity in towns like Kirkland Lake, Timmins and Sudbury, where every time an individual purchases a new antenna for a radio the local R.C.M.P. undercover agent travels around the neighbourhood asking such questions as "Why is the individual putting up such a high tower?" "What kind of short wave radio receiver does the individual have?" "What do the neighbours think he might be listening to?" and many other similar silly questions. I suggest if the officer wishes to find the answers to these questions he would be much more likely to accomplish his purposes by directing them to the individual himself or the individual who sold him the radio and antenna in the first place. I suggest that the individual is perhaps listening to police calls, or short-wave broadcasts in a language with which he is more familiar than that which is used by the local radio stations. I suggest these things do happen, and accomplish nothing in the way of security in this country, but only make a lot of people angry, including myself.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: You may go ahead and laugh but I suggest that many members of this house have been investigated by this security group at one time or another.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We cannot help but laugh when you talk such nonsense as you have been talking in regard to radio aerials.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
The minister may know a great deal about the activities of his department, but I do not think he knows as much as he thinks he does. I suggest many things are happening in his department of which he

Supply-R.C.M.P.
is completely unaware. As an example, he may have noticed an individual sitting in the member's gallery for quite some time; he is not here now. I suggest he is not aware of all the activities of that individual. However, I do not think much can be gained by this exchange of pleasantries between the minister and myself.
I am interested in the situation which exists in this field, and feel that nothing will be accomplished or changed unless we make some comment about it. I have not as yet seen any indication as to how many people are involved in the work of this particular section, nor have I heard any indication as to what has been done in relation to the supposed situation which exists. Surely the minister should present a resume of the extent of communism in Canada today. In some ridings communist candidates have run in the elections and, as a result, the number of supporters is known. We know the number is very limited. On several occasions I have had a communist candidate run against me, and on those occasions I was aware of the number of supporters he had. I suggest that if we are going to accomplish anything in this field we must publicize the dangers involved in communism and the rate of its growth in Canada. In that way perhaps something could be done to prevent it spreading.
It is quite easy for people to get up and say that unions have communists in their ranks. Sometimes this is true, but most of the unions in this country have methods of weeding out the communists once they find out who they are. Most unions have clauses in their membership forms that prevent communists from holding any office.
These things are not said by the department. The minister does not go around and say that the unions are taking whatever steps they can to eliminate the problem. A few minutes ago he mentioned my own political party. In our membership form that every member must sign there is a clause which states that he is not a member of any other political party. This does not really mean that we do not want a Conservative to join the C.C.F. It does not mean that we do not want a Liberal to join the C.C.F. What it really means is that if a communist gets into our organization and we find out about it, we want to be able to throw him out.
We do this occasionally. I do not think the Conservatives throw them out, or the Liberals either for that matter. We do, and we use this method of doing it. When the minister says there have been communists in our

party, that is true. There have been communists in the C.C.F. party, but we have publicly thrown them out on a number of occasions.
The unions also have fought the communists and thrown them out of their organizations. In the mining area around Timmins, where I have been connected with union activities, we have spent a great deal of our own money to do this. We have spent a great deal of time and effort in this regard. But the point is that nothing is ever said about the work these organizations do to get rid of communists. The menace, if you wish to call it that, is contained. No; it is much easier to get up and say, as some of the ministers have said, "Let us destroy the ban the bomb organization because there may be some communists in it".
Who said that? Be specific and responsible. Who said it?
He could not be either.
Who said it? Don't just stand there. That is a serious charge.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Stand up and ask a question if you wish to do so.
I will ask a question. Would the hon. member name the ministers who said "We will destroy the ban the bomb movement"?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Maybe I should not have said "destroy". I am referring to the discussion that has taken place in the house, for instance, in relation to the statement made by the Minister of National Defence to the reserve services in Winnipeg. I refer both to what was said there and the answers that have been given to questions about the matter.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: It has no relation to the argument going on today.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
It has to this extent. If there is a communist subversive movement which is dangerous to Canada in connection with this organization I am sure the branch would have taken a look at it, just as they have in the case of many other organizations. All I am saying is that much more could be done if the department were willing to help these organizations rid themselves of any communist influence. It does not seem to me that they are doing this as long as these matters are kept under cover. This branch is quite likely to grow in numbers because if you appoint one person to check on somebody's politics you have to assign two people to watch the first man to see that he is doing what he was supposed to do and is doing it in the proper manner. If this branch is not open to scrutiny, it can grow considerably.

In the mines we always knew that there were men working with us who were in fact employees of the management. We knew this and nobody seemed to care. If a man could pick up an extra $10 or $20 doing this kind of work then it was all the better for him. Nobody was particularly worried about it. Those miners who were communists admitted that they were, and quite often when they said they were communists they did not have the faintest idea what communism meant. In this regard I have known one or two cases of people who, after having been in Canada for 20 or 30 years, went back to their homelands and then moved heaven and earth to try to get back to Canada because they found they were more rebellious under the regime in their home country than they were under the regime in this country. They were really malcontents rather than people having any particular political philosophy.
I think some change of attitude should take place with regard to the security branch. It is all right for the branch to grow and do its work under cover, but I think the minister should occasionally make a report as to the dangers, because communism is a very different form of politics from any to which we are accustomed. As I understand the communist philosophy, the object is to establish an international organization that will control the world on an international basis. This is completely foreign to any other political philosophy of which I am aware. For this reason I think the minister and the department could assist the Canadian people considerably if they would stop creating a bogey as to this matter and really present the facts as they are. As long as people are kept in the dark it will be very difficult to find out what is going on, and this will lead to abuses and placing more emphasis on the situation than it really deserves.
I agree that the minister has a responsibility in this regard in that he has to exercise considerable discretion, but I think he will agree with me that the people who gather this information must be highly trained and skilled and be completely versed in the political aspect of their duties. I suggest that more education along this line is required than many of these men now have. It may be that this information should not be assessed by the R.C.M.P., as the minister says, and that in the security field the function of the R.C.M.P. is to gather facts and not to pass judgment on those facts. That responsibility rests elsewhere, primarily with the government.
This is the crux of the whole matter, Mr. Chairman. If the information obtained is not factual, if it is the pipe dream of some constable who thinks he has discovered a real
Supply-R.C.M.P.
hot spy ring because somebody has erected an abnormally high radio antenna, the facts will then be presented in such a manner as to convey an altogether wrong impression to people in the government. It is for this reason that I think more discretion should be exercised. Frankly, I think more information should be given as to what the threat is in Canada, how to fight it properly and in what manner the general public can be of assistance. The electors of Canada can solve the problem and eliminate whatever threat the communist party may pose in a political sense and so far as the rights that Canadians now enjoy are concerned. It seems to me that as long as communism is legal we are going to have to admit that not everyone who says he supports the communist party is a dangerous person, but may be simply supporting a particular political party.
There is some difference between these people and those who are operating in what we would call the spying field, obtaining information for the use of other countries. I suggest, as a result of my limited experience in this field, that most of the people who talk about communism have not the faintest notion what it is. Communism has been a bogey that has been thrown out. I am reminded of the story we used to have in primary school about crying wolf too often, and then nobody will listen.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
May I attempt to deal with some of the things that have been said, because if they go unanswered the impression may be created that there is no answer. The hon. member, if he reflects and will follow me, I believe will agree that he has indulged in so many exaggerations on the one hand, and inconsistencies on the other, that it is difficult to know what accusations he is trying to make.
The hon. member started out by saying there is no communist threat in Canada; that this was all nonsense; that we were really making too much out of this security and intelligence work. A little later he was saying that there is a communist threat and that the greatest credit should be given to the unions and to his own party for their work in finding out the communists and throwing them out of their movement.
It is difficult to know, therefore, what point of view the hon. member presents. If communists are persons whom we should ignore; if we should do nothing about checking on them, then I find it difficult to understand why he gives so much credit to the unions and his own party when they find communists within their ranks and throw them out. I happen to agree with the unions, and with the point of view of his party, when

Supply-R.C.M.P.
they say communists should not be allowed to infiltrate. I hope, therefore, that this last position of the hon. member is his true position; that he will agree that communism is a threat, and that Canada is entitled, indeed has an obligation, to protect herself against that threat and find out the extent and effectiveness of the threat.
Now, let me emphasize that in respect of security and intelligence, Canada runs no espionage service. Canada runs only a counterintelligence service. The work of the security and intelligence branch in Canada is exclusively confined to counter-intelligence. I doubt if any reasonable Canadian would deny that Canada is entitled to protect herself against espionage and, therefore, is entitled to take such proper measures as can be taken to determine the extent of the threat of espionage and of subversive movements within our midst.
In case there should be any doubt as to whether these communists are a threat, let me refer my hon. friend and the committee to the recent case in the United Kingdom. Canadian passports came to light in that case, and it took our highly competent, highly equipped and well staffed laboratory three days of intensive study to determine whether or not they were forgeries. I am advised that the proper expression would be that the whole documents were counterfeit. I do not want to give any misinformation here, and what I wish to say is that the Canadian passports had been so skilfully counterfeited that unless they were submitted to the crime detection laboratory for examination, no one could detect that they were counterfeit.
1 could cite a number of other cases, but I should like to emphasize that these passports were in the possession of persons who were convicted of espionage in circumstances which establish that there was a highly organized and, up to that time, successful espionage ring. These and other circumstances known to us, some of which have been made public and some of which should not be made public, are sufficient proof if proof were wanted that there is an organized subversive effort going on in Canada, which is part of an international plan of espionage.
As I say, I give full credit to organizations such as the hon. member's own party with respect to their detection and ejection of communists from their movement. I have given the same credit to the unions. I would say that this portion of his remarks simply establishes the necessity for the security and intelligence work which is being carried out. The hon. member did, unfortunately, indulge in some exaggeration which created a completely wrong impression. Let us take, for

instance, the suggestion he made that in a town like Timmins or Kirkland Lake the Royal Canadian Mounted Police investigated every case where an aerial was put up. This is what my hon. friend said, and he criticized us because he said we were doing such ridiculous things, going around making inquiries of the neighbours and at the store where the aerial was purchased. The reason we laughed was that the hon. member was talking nonsense.
Let me discuss what may happen. I would doubt very much whether such investigations were made in the course of security and intelligence work. I do not deny that there may have been some. Certainly I admit that such investigations are made from time to time. However, it must be remembered that we are responsible for investigations carried out on behalf of the Department of Transport under their act and regulations. These regulations state that a person must have a licence before he can operate a transmitting station. If we see an unusually high aerial being erected, this may well be used for the purpose of transmission. It is not related at all to security and intelligence, but a routine inquiry might have been made under the responsibility we have to ensure that there are no unlicensed transmitting sets being installed and operated in Canada.
The danger of an unbalanced view being taken of these things does not rest, by any means, upon the administration alone. I suggest that my hon. friend has clearly illustrated that there is an unbalanced and unduly suspicious mind in other quarters, as well as undue prejudice against the activities of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, particularly the security and intelligence branch. It is true there are some people, you know, who epitomize that well known expression of seeing a communist under every bed. This is, of course, stupid and exaggerated. There are, on the other hand, people who see a Royal Canadian Mounted policeman under every bed, and I suggest this is equally stupid and exaggerated thinking.
My hon. friend has suggested that the minister and the department are trying to create an overweight monster. I can assure my hon. friend, speaking personally, that my efforts are all the other way. Sometimes I have not been completely successful, and I have taken steps to deal with it. Certainly I have no desire to create or to be any overweight monster, and 1 have exerted every effort to ensure that security or intelligence work would not get out of hand. As I said earlier, we will not be able to carry out this or any other branch of police work without occasionally making mistakes. I think I am entitled to ask, however, that mistakes or alleged mistakes be drawn to our attention first, so

we can investigate them to ascertain whether there is anything that should be done to improve our methods.
I am sure the hon. member will agree, if he considers and analyses what he has said, that there have been inconsistencies in his complaints because of the credit he gives to those who take steps to eject communists from their own organizations, and he will agree that in fact there is a communist threat. He will agree that the government of Canada, through its security forces, have as much, indeed greater, responsibility than his own party and the labour unions to find out where the communists are, what they are doing and prevent them from doing harm, to the extent that that is possible.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: With respect to the difference of opinion concerning the subjects dealt with in my remarks, let me say that it was not my intention in the first portion of my comments to indicate that there was a threat. I was relating my remarks to what the minister said yesterday. When asked how many communists there are in Canada the minister said, using Tim Buck's own figure, there are 3,000. If we multiplied that number by one hundred there would be no political problem-
The hon. member must be crazy.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Well, if there were 300,000 communists how would that affect federal elections in Canada? I appreciate the minister's position. I feel that he made an honest assessment of the situation. My remarks related to the figure of 3,000 communists to which he referred. I do not think that is any threat in a political sense. I do not feel that the communists are going to form the government of Canada tomorrow or in the immediate future. With respect to antennae, I did not say that every time one went up-

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Unfortunately my hon. friend did say that. That is why I felt it necessary to correct him.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I did not intend to say that, and if I did I should correct that statement. The hon. member for Timmins brought a case to my attention. He lives next door to a fellow who put up a fairly high antenna and an investigation was made. In a community the size of Timmins there would be only a limited number of retail outlets selling long and short wave equipment. It would not have been difficult to inquire from the purchase source about the type of equipment bought, and an investigation would not have been necessary. I have no quarrel with the minister's remarks.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I wish to deal with one other matter, Mr. Chairman, because I feel the
Supply-R.C.M.P.
record should be set straight. I refer to the incident at the airport in Ottawa. I am advised that because of the point at which this vehicle was parked it was necessary to make an effort to move it. The vehicle could not be permitted to remain there because it was obstructing traffic. I am also advised that our member spoke politely to the lady in question, and upon being informed that she was ill he quickly withdrew and the vehicle was moved. I am also informed that the husband of the lady in question has indicated that he is perfectly satisfied with the approach, attitude and conduct of our member.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I raised it because of what was stated in a newspaper article. I had an almost identical experience myself.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: My point is that if my hon. friend had made inquiries of me or the commissioner he would have received a full explanation. It is well known that newspapers sometimes publish things they do not themselves check because they make good news at the time. Newspapers are interested in circulation, and reporters are busy and do not always have time to check the stories before they publish them. I do not wish to suggest that members of parliament are not also busy, but one might expect that they would be a little more inclined to check stories before repeating them.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to bring this discussion back down to the level of the common, ordinary man and speak about something that is of vital interest in my riding. I see that the hour for the luncheon recess is approaching. Like other hon. members of the committee I have been sitting here for hours listening to wrangling about communism and other irrelevant matters at a time when we should have been discussing estimates pertaining to the R.C.M.P. and the functions they perform.
I compliment the R.C.M.P. on the splendid work they are doing. My remarks are intended to be constructive, and I offer them for the purpose of assisting and helping the R.C.M.P. I represent the Macleod riding in western Canada which is the cradle of the cattle ranching industry and especially all along the foothills area of the Rockies. The deployment of R.C.M.P. personnel in small nuclei in communities such as Fort Macleod, Claresholm, High River and others is a pattern which may fit in with the requirements of other parts of the country, but it does not meet the requirements of this area in terms of the proper administration of police work.

Would the hon. gentleman permit a question?

Supply-R.C.M.P.
I will when I am through. My time is just about up.
Oh, oh.
I suggest, sir, that we call it one o'clock. When .we resume and I have completed my remarks I shall be pleased to answer any questions the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate might wish to raise.
I was just going to ask, Mr. Chairman, whether the hon. member was bringing the discussion down to the level of the bull.
No, I was bringing it down to the level of the tail end of a codfish and applying it to the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate.
Mr. Chairman, before this item carries-
Mr. Chairman, I called it one o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: It is not one o'clock.
It is not one o'clock yet.
I wish to continue my remarks when we resume.
Oh, no; not more of the same.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I see that it is one o'clock now.
