speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 2.30 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, in resuming my remarks which were under way just before the lunch hour I shall only say a few additional words. As I have mentioned, these remarks are made in the spirit of being helpful.
Before the luncheon adjournment I had been talking about police protection in the area which I represent. I had mentioned- and if I did not, I intended to do so-that there are police detachments at Fort Macleod, Claresholm and High River. I live in the area south of High River and northwest of Nan-ton. This area is out in the country.
The people of this area have been asking me for the past two years why there is not adequate police protection in the area. The distance between Claresholm and High River is about 50 miles, and if police protection is required, say at Connemara or Nan-ton, the police detachment, which is some 30 miles or more away at Claresholm, must be notified.

To give an illustration of the point I am attempting to make, at Connemara thieves broke into the United Grain Growers elevator about a month and a half ago. The theft took place during the night when the agent was not on duty, and when he returned to duty the next morning he found that the place had been broken into. He phoned the police detachment at Claresholm, but because of the pressure of other duties I suppose, or for some other reason, they did not get there until three o'clock in the afternoon. I could illustrate this point by mentioning other situations. All I am trying to say is that I think if the deployment of the men of the police force was examined, a better coverage of police protection could be provided in a given area without employing additional personnel.
I am asking the Department of Justice and the police force to re-examine this matter. In this particular area, as I mentioned this morning, there is a long stretch of foothill country running from away west and southwest of High River up as far as Banff, and then in the other direction clear down to the United States boundary line. In that area there is a large cattle ranching industry. The cattle ranchers who are living in the area are the most law-abiding citizens in Canada, but the odd thief comes around and butchers an animal.
What I wish to say is that if we had a little better coverage and if the police force that is now in that area were re-examined from the point of view of deployment, I think the people would be more satisfied because they would be given better police protection.
There are a few criticisms of this deployment that I might just as well mention. Some people say they never see a policeman out in the country; they are always going up and down the roads, two in a car. I have brought this to the attention of the Minister of Justice previously and nothing has happened. These people are criticizing the deployment of police personnel in relation to the amount of coverage which they would normally expect the police force to give.
It is quite possible that in terms of training and so on, it is necessary at times for two policemen to ride in a car, but as a general, day after day practice, it has opened the door to a pertain amount of criticism by local people. For this reason I should like the department to re-examine this particular aspect of the work of the police force.
There is another problem which I have raised before. At Waterton lakes there is a very large tourist trade in the summertime. People visit this area from the United States and other parts of Canada; in fact, they come in from all parts of the continent and the

world. I think it would be one of the finest advertisements for Canada if the police there were to wear scarlet uniforms.
I also suggest that the town police of Fort Macleod, where the old fort is situated, should be required to wear scarlet uniforms. This police force is paid for by the town of Fort Macleod and they police the town. The old fort has been resurrected there and people visit it by the thousands during the summertime. It is a replica of the original fort which the Royal Northwest Mounted Police established in 1874. I think that if any place in western Canada is appropriate for the wearing of scarlet uniforms by the police, it is the museum and fort at Fort Macleod.
Many tourists visit the fort. They do not see the scarlet uniform, and of course it is always a subject for questioning. One of the arguments used by those who oppose this suggestion is, "Well, it is the summertime; it is uncomfortable to wear the scarlet uniform. It is costly. You would not expect them to wear it on duty". They now call it a dress suit. Let me say that the traditional uniform has a particular place in the memory of the people of western Canada. The Royal Northwest Mounted Police policed that country for years and wore this same uniform so it is a bit late for anyone to begin arguing that it is uncomfortable to wear in the summer. Another argument against it is that it is warm. Well, it is not particularly warm at Waterton lakes, and even at Fort Macleod it is only warm for a few hours during the heat of the day. The scarlet uniform is worn by officers of the R.C.M.P. outside the parliament buildings. Advantage is being taken of it there for the benefit of the tourist trade. I am not asking for anything new. I am asking for something which the people out there have asked me to ask for, and I should like the minister to give this request his earnest and affirmative consideration.
I want to pay a compliment to the police officers operating in my area. The quality of the personnel who have been selected to work in that part of the country is very high. I think they are out to do a good job. Perhaps some of the weaknesses of the R.C.M.P. are the responsibility of the upper echelon. I would ask them not to be so resistant to the suggestions which are made, and to reexamine some of the things they are doing with a view to improving the effectiveness of the force in different parts of the dominion and particularly in the constituency which I represent.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Is part of Waterton lakes in his constituency?
Supply-R.C.M.P.

Yes, the Waterton lakes west of the fifth meridian are in my constituency. I might add that the hon. member for Lethbridge has the townsites and I have the fishing area. He has the problems and I have the pleasure.

There is one matter which I should like to raise and upon which I should like to hear a comment by the minister. I am asking the commissioner of the R.C.M. Police, through the Minister of Justice, if he can give us any information on R.C.M.P. planning as a result of the experience gained during Tocsin 61. On this civil defence exercise two backbenchers, one from the Liberal party, and myself, were privileged to be present. I am speaking only in relation to the R.C.M.P. phase of that exercise. With the exception of the room where the cabinet or the privy council met, the member who represented the Liberal party and myself were allowed to move everywhere we wished and to ask all the questions we wished. I found it most interesting, especially as far as the R.C.M. Police are concerned.
I am certain that the commissioner will remember that in the course of this realistic simulation of the bombing of Canada, he received, in his underground shelter during the course of that exercise, a message from the commissioner of the Ontario provincial police saying that half his men had become casualties and calling for assistance from the R.C.M.P. But the situation was that the R.C.M.P. had themselves lost two thirds of their number through casualties. The commissioner will remember that I was at his desk at that time. I give this as an indication of the situation which developed during this exercise, and on the basis of this situation I ask the minister to tell us what plans are being prepared to carry on the work and the responsibility of the R.C.M.P. should such a situation become a reality.
I admit this is a strange way in which to introduce this question, but the commissioner was there, together with his two assistants, and so was I. The exercise was designed to be a realistic study of survival possibilities and the situation which I have described is the one with which the commissioner found himself faced at his table at that underground point at Petawawa when the message came to him.

Before the minister answers that question I should like to ask another one. Can he give us any information about the use by the R.C.M.P. of writs of assistance? Can he tell us whether their use is restricted to certain divisions of the R.C.M.P. or whether all officers carry such documents

Supply-R.C.M.P.
with them. I recall, several years ago, reading an editorial which appeared in a British Columbia newspaper regarding an incident where an R.C.M.P. officer suspecting, after finding a stolen car, that the person who stole it was in a certain house, forced his way into that house and checked everyone in it.
I am concerned about these writs of assistance. I think bureaucracy can look after itself, but ordinary citizens need protection against the arbitrary use of such powers and that is why I am asking this question, although, of course, we all know that the police do need power in order to carry out their responsibilities. I think that the use of such instruments and powers should be very closely watched by those individuals who are in charge of the R.C.M. Police and the other forces which use these instruments and powers. I have the greatest respect and admiration for the R.C.M. Police and think that it is a magnificent body doing wonderful work. However, it is composed of individuals who are human and fallible, and unfortunate incidents do occur.
Finally, the last question I wish to ask is this. Where forcible entry is made and damage is done, and when no conviction is obtained, what recourse do individuals have to recover the cost of damages which have been incurred?

Mr. Chairman, as the last surviving ex-member of the R.C.M.P. in this house I should like to say a word or two about the force. We very often hear that the mounted police force is not the outfit it used to be. I do not think it is. I think it gets better year by year. Since I retired after 23 years service, some three years ago I have seen many changes made for the betterment of the force. I should like to refer in particular to the present commissioner, who is certainly one of the finest members ever produced by the force. I say that advisedly because he is a man who has come up through the ranks. His success in this regard is an indication to each recruit who joins the mounted police force that the highest positions are open to him if he combines his ambition with the necessary toil.
I recently had the privilege of witnessing a passing out parade at Rockcliffe. The excellent condition and the look of high morale on the faces of those individuals, particularly at this time when so much emphasis is being placed on physical fitness in this country, should be an inspiration to any young Canadian entertaining the idea of joining this force. I think the condition of those young men, who have completed their training, should be an inspiration to all the young 
people of this country who seek a high degree of physical fitness, and I suggest the high standard of the force should be emulated by all training establishments and schools across this country. I think the force generally, and those individuals in charge of it from the minister down to the fine N.C.O.'s, should be commended for the excellent work that is being done.
An efficient force of this kind operated and controlled by the government cannot be expected to maintain this excellent work without money. I know from experience that those in charge of this force must have adequate financial resources in order to implement the projects which they have very carefully thought out, and I know they have pared their expenses to the bone before asking for the appropriation. I know that those who make up the estimates give meticulous care to make sure that the taxpayers' money will not be wasted and, when they ask for expenditures, they are not subject to Parkinson's law but are asking for money which is absolutely essential. When the minister submits his full request for appropriation for the Royal Canadian Mounted Police I should like to appeal to all members of this committee to give unanimous support to the request for an appropriation to underwrite the costs of this important and well-carried out work. This department gives the taxpayer 100 cents for his dollar.

Mr. Chairman, the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were the original law enforcement body in western Canada. As one among a number of hon. members who knew the prairies in the earlier days, let me say that I appreciate fully the part that the force played. Reference has been made to the situation with regard to customs examination and also the wearing of scarlet uniforms, but originally the role of the force was to bring law and order to western Canada.
I should like to say to the minister, and through him to the commissioner, that in our part of the country we have the highest regard for the force and for its leadership. It is very easy to talk about scarlet uniforms or about entry into Canada through the customs ports. I suggest sincerely that these matters are not really germane to the role of the force. I do not believe the R.C.M.P. should be relegated to the role of undercover men. I believe the force should be preserved for their own particular role and that role in my opinion is the one they filled originally when the force was created late in the last century, to preserve law and order, which they have done in a magnificent way.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
I will deal with the questions that have been raised since I replied just before lunch. The hon. member for Macleod drew to the attention of the committee the fact that he has requested of us on a number of occasions that we make some changes in the points at which men are stationed. I must point out to him that the question of the organization and location of detachments is under constant review at headquarters. It is also under constant review at the headquarters in each province and, of course, where we operate as the provincial police

Supply-R.C.M.P.
force under contract it is under constant review by the attorney general of the province. Under these latter circumstances the primary responsibility in determining where detachments will be located and how they will be manned is that of the attorney general of the province.
It is just not possible for us to comply with every request that is made. From the police point of view such a request is looked at first having in mind efficiency of administration and policing. It is also a matter on which we are bound to consult with the attorney general where we are operating as the provincial force under contract as in Alberta. I can only suggest that probably in this case the proper place to start is with the attorney general of the province to get his view and/or recommendation on the change.
With regard to the wearing of the scarlet tunic by members of the detachment in Macleod, I must point out that they are doing the work of a municipal force under contract with the municipality. They are there as a municipal police force to do police work and not to be in their red tunics as a tourist or historic attraction. I am advised that we have had no request from the municipality of Macleod, with whom, as I say, we have a contract, for a change in the uniform or for our men to wear scarlet tunics in the summer or at any other time. On ceremonial occasions they will, of course, appear in their scarlet tunics, but on all other occasions and during all other times they are there because they are doing the work of a municipal police force under contract, and will be wearing their working uniform.
The situation on parliament hill is quite different. Here they are not doing the work of a straight police detachment. They are in no way similar to the detachment stationed at Macleod under contract. While I have to give this answer now and do not hesitate to give it, I hope it will not be taken as meaning that we are inflexible. Should the situation change at any time or should other considerations be laid before us, we will consider every request in that light but they must be considered first from the point of view of the efficient discharge of the function which the police are there to discharge.
The hon. member for Vancouver East asked me about the record as revealed by exercise Tocsin in 1961. He drew to our attention that for exercise purposes it was reported that two thirds of the members of the force were wiped out or rendered ineffective. The hon. member must realize, of course, that for exercise purposes Tocsin was designed to produce the maximum damage in Canada because it

was desired to exercise all regional headquarters as well as the central government headquarters. I am not saying that under no circumstances would there be attacks as heavy and effective as this was represented to be for exercise purposes, but I am simply saying that for the purpose of the exercise the narrative assumed very heavy and very effective attacks on practically every part of Canada. Under these circumstances there is no question but that the casualties would have been of the order which operationally the commissioner assumed as a result of the reports that came in.
The only answer we have and the only answer we can see-and we are planning on this basis now bearing this possibility in mind-is the establishment of auxiliaries and reserves in the larger centres. Then, in the event of damage from hostilities we would have a force in reserve that could quickly be sent in to take the place of the casualties. We cannot maintain these auxiliaries and reserves as an actual part of the strength of the force in advance of hostilities but arrangements must be made in advance so that we can call them up immediately to take the place of the casualties and to undertake some of the extra work which will fall upon the force in any event in time of war.
The hon. member for Vancouver South asked me about the number of men who would be in possession of writs of assistance. The answer to that is, a very limited number of senior personnel are in possession of writs of assistance and these personnel are confined to the drug squads and the personnel enforcing the Customs and Excise Act. A writ of assistance would not be used in connection with a search for a stolen motor car unless it was suspected the car had been used in connection with a drug or customs and excise offence. I can only tell the hon. member, therefore, that in so far as a search for a stolen vehicle is concerned, there must have been some error in the report which came to him. I should like to know the details, however, in case something did go wrong or something was used in a manner in which it should not have been used. If the hon. member would give me the details he has, then I could satisfy him as to whether or not his report is correct and satisfy myself as to action which should be taken if a mistake has been made.
I should point out also that there are a certain number of search warrants placed in the hands of our personnel by the attorneys general of the provinces in which we act as a provincial police force. However, in so far as writs of assistance are concerned, they are confined to senior personnel and even

then they are limited to the personnel doing work in connection with narcotics and customs and excise offences.
If damage is done in the course of the execution of a writ or a search, the policy is that where the damage done in the exercise of a writ under a federal statute is minor, it is paid for on the spot. If the damage is major, it is referred to the Department of Justice for submission to the treasury board for payment of the damage or at least that portion of it for which we could be said to be responsible. If damage is done in the course of the execution of a writ when we are acting as a provincial police force, then the policy regarding payment for the damage is decided by the provincial attorney general.
I am very appreciative of the remarks of the hon. member for Athabasca, recognizing that he had service in this force and recognizing the authority with which he speaks. Every effort will be made to continue to maintain the high standard of recruitment, performance and public relations which has come to be the hallmark of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The hon. member for Essex West renewed a request for the stationing of a member of the force at the port of entry at Windsor. He did refer to the fact that the figure of the mounted policeman in his scarlet tunic has become an established and accepted national symbol. In my opinion it is extremely significant that the figure of a policeman should occupy this place of affection in the public mind in what is certainly not a police state. This is a mark not only of the respect in which the force is held but of the recognition by the public that in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police we have a force with respect to whom there is no danger of their attempting to become the master of the public instead of their servants.
From one point of view, therefore, the temptation is always on those administering the force, and on the minister responsible, to do what we can to put men at strategic points in the scarlet tunic. However, we have always to remember what I said a moment ago. This force will not be respected if it does not approach every problem from the point of view of the efficient discharge of the duties for which it is responsible; that is their role, and not the mere "cashing in", as it were, on the traditions of the force and the respect in which the force is held.
At Windsor, we have a detachment of 17 uniformed members and two civil servants. We also have a 50-foot boat of the marine division with a crew of four. These men, of course, are engaged entirely upon federal work, primarily investigations under the Customs Act and the Immigration Act. I suppose
Supply-R.C.M.P.
that Windsor, being a city made up of normal Canadians, there is a certain amount of income tax work as well. In so far as the marine division is concerned, and indeed the regular members of the force, they have also the enforcement of the small boat regulations. I am advised that we have never been requested by the customs or immigration departments to have members stationed at the actual port of entry. The responsibility at ports of entry, of course, is principally that of the customs and excise branch and the immigration service. They do all the port of entry work and we, in turn, make all the investigations which they request of us and which may arise out of the work they do. I do suggest for consideration of hon. members this thought, that whether or not we were to have men in the red tunic or just in ordinary working dress of the police, would it in fact be wise to have a policeman stationed at your port of entry? I cannot think of any other country, the United States or elsewhere- I may be wrong-where a person going through the port of entry is met by a police officer. It is always the customs officer or the immigration officer.
One of my colleagues reminds me that there may be some countries where one sees police at the borders, but these are not the countries operating under our system of government. I do raise the question of whether it would be wise for us to station a police officer in a port of entry. My own view would be that there are many considerations which argue against it. As long as you have police, as we have at Windsor and other ports of entry, who are available close at hand to make investigations or undertake enforcement work should the work of a police officer be necessary, I think that is all we should do. We should not embark on a policy of actually stationing them in the vicinity, or rather in the building through which immigrants are passing.
I thank the hon. member for Medicine Hat and all hon. members for the indication of their support for these estimates.

There is one further question I should like to ask the Minister of Justice. This is a subject which has concerned a great many members of the House of Commons. Could the Minister of Justice explain the jurisdiction and responsibility of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on parliament hill? I raise this question because of an incident which occurred. I realize that inside the House of Commons the responsibility is that of our own security police. We never see the mounted police inside the House of Commons building itself, except during visits by President Kennedy or other distinguished guests. However, we do find

Supply-R.C.M.P.
the Royal Canadian Mounted Police on the grounds of parliament hill. Beyond the grounds we take it that the responsibility is that of the Ottawa police itself.
The reason I raised the matter is this. There has Altered through to a great many members of the House of Commons news of an incident of not so many days ago where an employee in the House of Commons had his car parked within the House of Commons area. After we adjourned at 10:30 p.m. at night, on going down to enter his car, he found somebody trying to break into it. He chased the man but could not catch him. However, he had a good description of him. He naturally came back to the R.C.M.P. in the grounds and, according to the information that I know has been given to a great many members in this house, he was told, "Get in touch with the Ontario police".
The incident happened inside the House of Commons grounds. So although within a few minutes of the time of the incident he could describe the man who had escaped and who had been trying to get into his car, he was told by the R.C.M.P. "That is a matter for the Ontario police and the Ottawa municipal police". As a result of that occurrence which is known to a great many members, I ask this question. Just what is the jurisdiction, authority and responsibility of the R.C.M.P. as distinguished from that of our security police who are most magniAcent and who are doing a wonderful job in the House of Commons inside the building, the R.C.M.P. in the grounds and the Ottawa and municipal police outside the gates? From discussions I have had about this matter I am certain that we would appreciate any information we can get upon this point.

It sometimes puzzles me a great deal indeed that matters of this sort are reserved for the estimates and then one is expected to discuss the matter in detail without ever having heard of the case. As I have tried to indicate, I would greatly appreciate it if, at any time an hon. member has a ground for complaint or a ground for being disturbed or concerned, he would bring the matter to my attention either directly or through my oAice or through my department or take it up with the commissioner. He would And us fully prepared to believe that our men are human and can make mistakes and anxious to rectify those mistakes or any situation which gave rise to those mistakes.
But I am unable to give a full answer on this particular matter because I have not heard of it previously. If it was a matter of such great concern to members or to the staff or personnel of the house, I regret that it has not been taken up with one of the persons who has the prime responsibility in

the matter such as myself. However, that situation does not alter the fact that, having now heard about it, I shall most certainly look into it. I shall be grateful if the hon. member will give me the particulars such as the date and so on. If the situation as described does in fact exist, I would say that one of the members of the force-inadvertently, I hope-has made an error in his approach. I think that we should under circumstances such as were outlined, and at all times, be prepared in the force to give every assistance within our power, including taking details and reporting to the superiors in the force itself and establishing ourselves any liaison that may be necessary with other police forces. I can only express regret if that was not done in the situation described by my hon. friend.
With regard to the situation generally I would say this. On parliament hill, on government of Canada property, the R.C.M.P. are responsible for the enforcement of the Government Property Traffic Act and of course, here as everywhere else, for the enforcement of all other federal statutes. The Government Property Traffic Act is the authority under which the parking regulations on parliament hill are enacted, although these regulations are worked out in conjunction with the Speakers of the two houses. The authority of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, however, extends only to the outside precincts such as the driveways and parliament hill outside the parliament buildings themselves. Inside the authority rests with the protective staff who operate directly under Mr. Speaker.
I understand that the Ontario provincial police take the position that, in the case of any crime committed under the Criminal Code, even on parliament hill, they reserve the right or the residual authority under the constitutional position that the responsibility for the enforcement of the Criminal Code within the province rests with the attorney general. I do not think that any real point of difficulty has ever arisen. Certainly if a man were detected in the commission of a crime we would not take the absurd position that we have to send out for the Ontario provincial police, nor would they expect us to do so. We would act immediately and then turn over the offender or the information to the Ontario provincial police or the Ottawa police. This is why, if the circumstances are as they have been outlined, I regret that attitude was not taken. I think we would be expected to take the particulars at once and hand them over to the Ontario provincial police for their assistance so that co-operatively we might work together in the apprehension of any offender.

That is, however, the general situation. But with regard to the commission of crimes, even in this area-I refer to crimes under the Criminal Code-the Ontario provincial police say they have the right and that they prefer that, having done everything we are required to do at the moment, we turn the information over to them for the ultimate enforcement of the law.
Is it correct that you have one room in the east block to which the R.C.M.P. officer can take somebody he picks up on the hill? Have you one room in the east block with bars?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We have a member stationed at the east block inside the south entrance. He is on duty during the daylight hours. I do not believe we have any room in that building.
Is that a jail?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: No. We have no jail on parliament hill unless, of course, my hon. friend regards this chamber as a jail.

No. I asked that question because I saw a man picked up. I do not know why he was picked up. He was taken away by the police and I think he was put in one room in the east block. Is there one room in the east block where you put anybody who is picked up?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I have never heard of one. This is perhaps another example of the situation I have mentioned. When my hon. friend hears of these extraordinary and unusual circumstances I wish he would bring them to my attention at the time. Then I should be able to give him an answer. I know of no room. The commissioner here knows of no room. I have been in and out of that building a score of times and I have seen no room. I have seen a corporal on duty there. They have a little hallway that they use but there is no jail on parliament hill.

I have just one question to ask the minister. In view of the situation of the lobster fishermen in district No. 7 this spring, where fishing only started in some
Supply-Fisheries
cases around June 1 and where a full month was lost, would the minister advise the committee whether he has received any requests either for an extension of the present season beyond July 1 or for a month's extra fishing later in the fall?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, there have been numerous requests directly from fishermen, and some have been conveyed to me by hon. members. Perhaps I may make a brief statement on the general situation.
There have been requests brought to my attention for an extension in district No. 4. These requests were made not only by fishermen but by the hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg and the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare. The situation was very carefully reviewed and it was found that in this district, which has had an open season for quite a long period of time, the catch was about the average of the last few years. Therefore the request was denied.
The hon. members from Halifax and Anti-gonish-Guysborough conveyed requests to me from fishermen in that area, and there have been many other direct requests for an extension of the lobster fishing season in district No. 5, which would normally close on June 20. I am recommending that the season in this district be extended to June 30.
With regard to district No. 7B and district No. 9, the season in district No. 7B has already been extended five days, to July 5. It is too early yet to determine whether or not we should further extend the season. Requests have been received for its extension, but it is too early yet to make a determination because this will be dependent on two conditions; one is extent of the catch during the remainder of this month, and the other is what the water temperatures will be and in what condition the lobsters themselves will be when July 5, or whatever date is applicable, arrives. Dependent on those two conditions, near the closing date we will make a determination as to whether or not it will be possible, if necessary, to extend the season.
We have received a few requests, from individuals only as far as I know, that instead of extending the seasons in these districts at this time of year they should be closed at the normal time and a short season opened in the fall. This refers to districts where the season is not normally open in the fall.
This does not seem to have general support. I would not be inclined to recommend the opening of a fall season in these districts, because it is my understanding that this was tried on one occasion in the past in similar circumstances-this was quite a few years ago-and as a result, or at least in part as a result, the catches for the following years

Supply-Fisheries
in the districts were not good. Therefore on balance I think the suggestion of a fall season would be of no general benefit to the fishermen concerned.

Mr. Chairman, the minister has mentioned that there has already been an extension for district 7B until July 5. Will the minister give some consideration to extending the season in this district to July 8, if the water temperature is appropriate and the quality of the lobster is still good, because it will give the fishermen the full benefit of a week in July; otherwise they would have to stop in the middle of the week.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: It is too early to make a determination in this matter, but certainly as these requests come in they will be given very careful and close consideration.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to call the attention of the minister to conditions in the waters just outside the port of Vancouver. Just today I received a letter which says, among other things, that the debris in Howe sound covers an area of acres and acres; that one has to pick one's way through this debris and in spite of doing this hulls are dented and scratched, propellers are ruined and cooling systems are plugged.

We have put teeth in the Fisheries Act and this sort of thing has got to be stopped. It is the function of this department to stop it.
This sort of condition about which you read in the newspapers and about which people write to you is, I think, shameful, not only in regard to spoiling perhaps the finest boating ground in North America, but it also affects the matter of conservation. I think conditions are getting worse out there and the department has got to take action, and drastic action. I would like some report as to what the department is going to do.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a few words on this item dealing with conservation and development. I have attempted to look at this problem objectively and I have sought advice from people connected with the fishing industry as primary producers, buyers, processors and exporters. Today we live in a technical world. Science has advanced by leaps and bounds, and in

this advance the fishing industry has been swept along. New and better methods have been devised to catch fish of all species. Where once the location of dense concentrations of fish was a matter of chance, the science of electronics today minimizes this element and pinpoints with 100 per cent proficiency the concentration of fish, so much so that mother nature is waging a losing battle in order to maintain a proper balance.
Lobster, the basis of that great Nova Scotia industry, has not fared any better in its attempt for survival. Assuredly the lobster remains the prey of its natural enemy. This has been its battle down through the ages. Seagulls continue to delight in the appetizing lobster egg that floats for seven days on the surface of the ocean where it drifts aimlessly. The codfish and his colleagues devour their share of these eggs. It has never been determined what percentage of eggs laid by the female lobster do develop into mature lobsters. Even when the surviving floating eggs sink to the bottom and become baby lobsters, fish of all species delight in swallowing them whole. So, as may be seen, the fight for survival goes on.
But this fight is made more difficult because man has jumped into the fray and, over the period of years, devised ingenious methods of trapping lobsters. Before the birth of electronic devices and with the assistance of the Department of Fisheries regulations for protection, it appeared that the lobster population was holding its own in count, in size, and quality. But now depth sounders, fish-scopes-and what have we not in electronic devices-have turned the tide of battle in favour of the fishermen.
Perusal of fisheries statistics reveals, with weather conditions similar in nature in various years, that the catch remains almost at a constant level. But the same statistics fail to take into account that more fishermen have turned to lobster fishing and that each individual fisherman must use an increased number of traps in order to maintain his catch average. This necessarily results in a smaller take-home pay cheque and it also means a depletion of lobster grounds heretofore never fished by the fishermen. Boats wander farther out to sea in search of lobsters and this successfully, because electronics permit them to find shoals never before fished. Years long gone by it was a common occurrence for offshore fishermen to land 50 to 60 pounds of oversized lobster, that is, lobsters over five inches in carapace measurement and ranging from five to 11 pounds. Today this is of rare occurrence. And in this process of depleting the stock of the oversized lobsters, one can readily understand and appreciate how this necessarily curtails
Supply-Fisheries
productivity. It has been determined that an oversized female lobster bears as many as 100,000 eggs.
Different and varied proposals have been advanced in order to lend mother nature a helping hand in halting this depletion of lobster population. Season dates have been jockeyed around to the point where it now appears that nothing further can be done to satisfy nature's requirements and, in the meantime, safeguard the fishermen's best interest. Lobster hatcheries have been advocated, but past experience shows them not to have been too successful. I am of the firm belief that we should let mother nature perform her time-honoured duties and that we should curtail man's illegal encroachments. Patrol service should be stepped up. The consumption of undersized lobsters today is alarming and although man realizes fully that market lobsters are wholly dependent on the preservation of the baby population it seems that the temptation for this forbidden fruit is too great. A more adequate program of protection seems here the only solution. This would greatly assist mother nature in her preservation schedule. But in order to lend the greatest possible assistance to mother nature, I would urge the Minister of Fisheries to take a long and searching look at the feasibility of henceforth returning to the Atlantic waters lobsters over five inches in carapace measurement. I would also strongly urge that all female lobsters bearing eggs be purchased by the federal government to become its property, and be sufficiently marked so as to permit the fisherman to return them with certainty to the water and make it more difficult for him to offer them for sale. A conservation effort of this kind would not be costly and it would be of greater value than all the hatchery schemes which might be evolved. From the very start it would prevent the too great depletion of the lobster population presently being brought about by man's ambitions, yet of his necessity.
I was amazed the other day to hear a statement in the House of Commons that the sale of fish is declining. What amazed me most was that the onus for the decline was being placed on the shoulders of the Department of Fisheries. I cannot go along with this assertion for the simple reason that I believe the responsibility for increasing the sale of fish in Canada must be shared by the primary producer, the buyer, the processor, the wholesaler, the retailer and the one who prepares the fish. In the case of the primary producer there is still room for improvement. These are facts which I can bear out from my personal observation and I am sure hon. members who live close to the sea will agree with me if they have gone down to the

Supply-Fisheries
wharves and watched the boats coming in with their fish. I am sure many of them will have detected, though, fortunately, it is only in a minority of cases, the uncleanness of the fish which are aboard certain boats. In one case I noticed, a tub was filled with water to wash the fish, the fish were dressed in that tub, washed in the same water and finally left there until the boat reached shore to sell that fish. Assuredly this practice does not lend itself to the production of the best tasting fish products.
The buyers of fish products also have problems. If the primary producer does not practice care in dealing with the product, he is not able to offer the cleanest and best fish possible. I have noticed, as I am sure many other hon. members from ridings with fishing industries have, that fish is often left to lie on wharves where flies can get at them, and where the sun glares down. I have known of instances where fish have been allowed to sit in the back of trucks for a whole day before being processed at night.
That does not happen in British Columbia.

I suggest the processors and wholesalers must depend a great deal on primary producers in order to offer for sale the best product available. If they do not receive the best fish under the best possible conditions, they can not in turn sell the product.
I should also like to state that no matter how well the fish is finally prepared for sale, how sanitary the conditions under which it has been stored and processed, if the cook is not able to cook it properly, the efforts of those involved in bringing this fish to market are lost. In this nation, which should be a leader in the processing and cooking of fish, we have fallen down miserably, and I, therefore, cannot place this blame upon the Department of Fisheries. I am aware of the very noble efforts of the Department of Fisheries directed toward teaching fishermen to use the most efficient methods possible to handle their product. I am also aware of the efforts of the Department of Fisheries in setting up test kitchens to encourage the elegant art of fish cuisine but I am sure hon. members will not have to search far to find an example of ill-prepared food.

Mr. Chairman, a few moments ago I asked the minister a question. In reply he informed me that the pollution of water by sawdust and debris in Howe sound came within the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport. In checking the Fisheries Act, which has just recently been before this house, I find that the Department of Fisheries

is given power in regard to obstruction or pollution of waters frequented by fish. Returning to my original point, I should like to state that the director of the department at Vancouver should take more effective action than has been taken to date to clean up this pollution of the waters around the city of Vancouver. I do not think the responsibility in this regard falls on the Department of Transport, but rests entirely upon the shoulders of the officials of the Department of Fisheries. I should like the minister to explain why he stated that this subject is under the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, perhaps I did not make myself sufficiently clear when I replied to the hon. member. What I did intend to imply was that I would look into the matter, as far as it is my responsibility to do so. I suggested that the Department of Fisheries had a responsibility in respect of pollution of waters which is deleterious to fish. I did not intend to suggest that it was not the Department of Fisheries' responsibility in that respect, and that as far as it is a responsibility of the department, everything possible will be done to correct the situation. I did say, however, that the Department of Transport also had a certain responsibility in regard to pollution of navigable waters, and that would include Howe sound. I will certainly collaborate with my colleague to see that the matter is looked into and corrected as far as possible.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman,
first I wish to say that I neglected to say the last time I was on my feet that I will certainly take under consideration the observations made by the hon. member for Shel-burne-Yarmouth-Clare. With regard to the points raised by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, I wish to assure him that the salmon regulations for Newfoundland are under an intensive review by the department at the present time. As he indicated, these regulations were taken over holus-bolus under the Fisheries Act and are regulations that were designed and brought into effect at various times over the years in a piecemeal way. We are reviewing them at the present time to try to make them as reasonable as possible.
With regard to the question of an arbitrary line on one side of which salmon nets have to be lifted on the week end, that is also included in what I have just said, but I want to point out that the purpose of the weekend lift in theory anyway is to allow the

Supply-Fisheries
escape of salmon for purposes of reproduction and so that the salmon migrating on the week ends will reach their destination successfully. There are many features about this matter which perhaps do not meet the objective and, as I said, this question is also being reviewed. If the regulations are having the result that the hon. member has outlined, this does not make sense, of course. I have no doubt that may be the case at least in part and I assure him that the matter is being carefully reviewed at the present time.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a brief word regarding sport salmon fishing in Newfoundland and conservation and the regulations applied thereto. As everybody knows, sport salmon fishing is a very great tourist attraction in Newfoundland, and it does appear to me as well as to many others that over the last few years sufficient protection has not been given to the industry with the result that the industry is not being conserved in the way it should be.
I know it is impossible for the department to place a river guardian at every bend of every river but I believe it is necessary to increase the protection now being given with regard to the enforcement of the salmon regulations, particularly on the west coast of Newfoundland. I suggest to the minister that a survey be made of the protection now being provided with a view to improving the service and maintaining a protection service on every river that will stop some of the illegal fishing now being carried on.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we have also realized the necessity of having greater protection on our fishing streams generally in the maritimes and especially in Newfoundland. We are making an effort to have an increase in next year's estimates for this purpose so that a greater degree of protection can be given on these various streams.
The whole question of the conservation of the Atlantic salmon is a complicated one because in some cases there is a division of interest between the sport fishermen on the one hand and the commercial fishermen on the other and in addition the salmon have no regard for provincial boundaries. Many of the fish that migrate to Quebec, New Brunswick and Nova Scotia pass by Newfoundland and for that reason there has been established a committee of the senior officials of the fisheries departments of the Atlantic provinces and our own officials to try to correlate the regulations in all these areas so that the proper degree of conservation will be achieved with the result, we hope,

that not only will the Atlantic salmon population be maintained but will even be increased both for sport fishing and for commercial fishing.

148. Destruction of dogfish and other predators, $150,000.

My remarks, Mr. Chairman, will be directed to great lakes fishing. I should like to ask the minister what progress is being made in the control of the lamprey eel. The lamprey eel came into the great lakes about 20 years ago and has multiplied tremendously. It has been a big factor in the destruction of lake trout in Georgian bay and also in lake Erie.
I should like the minister to explain what progress is being made in controlling this cannibal fish, and at the same time perhaps he could comment on the smelts. This is also a salt water fish which came into the lakes a few years ago. While it has some commercial value, the fishermen are becoming quite concerned about it because it is spreading so rapidly they are afraid it will eliminate some of the better class of fish from the great lakes.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
At an earlier date in my estimates, Mr. Chairman, I did make a statement regarding the progress in lamprey control in the great lakes. I can say that it is very encouraging. The scientists have been able to discover a specific poison for the lamprey which kills the lamprey but does not injure other forms of life. This is being used extensively at the present time. It is a little early yet to assess properly the success we are meeting with this program. However, by next year we should be able to say categorically or nearly so whether or not this is going to be successful, as we hope it will. Then, there is the general question of restoring the
Supply-Fisheries
balance of life in the lakes after the lamprey are controlled. I think that is all I need to say at this moment.
I now have the information with regard to the price of bait at Burgeo. 1 find that we do not have a bait depot at Burgeo, so the price referred to must be the price charged by a private firm.
With regard to the question asked by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo, would this particular firm be entitled to a rebate on the bait assistance?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: It is not a question of a rebate, it is a question of a grant which is earned in a period of 10 years if certain services, up to the standards set by the department, are provided by the firm concerned. This grant is not reflected directly in the price of the bait sold.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext:
I, too, wanted to inquire about the progress in the control of the lamprey eel in the great lakes area. I was very interested in it. A few years ago, there was evidence that this lamprey eel was continuing to spread into other areas and that was the reason for my interest. Four or five years ago, I was told that the method for exterminating them was electric shock. Barriers had been established throughout the lake Superior area as well as lake Huron. Statements were made that there would be a much better method for destroying them shortly, but they were under control.
I notice there has been no increase in the amount of money authorized for this purpose. It would seem to me that $150,000 is not a large sum of money to be spent controlling a fish that has such a devastating effect. It spreads very rapidly. It eliminates all the fish with which it comes in contact. It seems to me that we should not wait for a year and a half in order to assess the situation. It seems to me that we should devote more money to getting rid of it now. It will be easier to do it now than it will be a couple of years from now.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext:
I believe the hon. member may be labouring under a misunderstanding. The vote on which this discussion started is item 148 and it does not really apply to the destruction of lamprey. The money provided for that purpose is in item 150. It is a much greater amount than the $150,000 referred to. The chemical destruction of lamprey is being carried on at a high rate. Finances are not a limiting factor at the moment. All of the lampricide that can feasibly be used at the present time is being used this year in a very heavy program that is going on both in Canada and in the United States as far as the destruction of lamprey

Supply-Fisheries
in the lakes are concerned, it is a total of $424,000. That is the Canadian share of this item making a total, with the United States share, of $1,300,000.
As I said earlier, it is a little bit too early to be definite about the success of this program but it looks to be very encouraging indeed. The electric barriers to which the hon. member referred are still being used but not primarily to control the lamprey. They are being used as a counting device to determine the success of the poisoning process used in the streams for the destruction of lamprey. Poisoning has a great advantage. When the eggs are laid in these streams, the larva takes about five years to develop before the young lamprey migrate back to the lakes. With the lampricide method you wipe out five-year stocks in one fell swoop whereas in the other method you can only control the mature lamprey or each year's crop of small lamprey coming down. This looks very encouraging. However, I think I should not say more at the moment.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I am appreciative of the statement the minister has made. Can he explain how the system is working out, how the bait is laid down or the process that is being used in relation to the spreading of this lampricide? What I am curious about is this. Does it leave any opportunity for co-operation and assistance of the municipalities which showed a great deal of interest in the control that originally was implemented through the electric barrier method?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries
speechtext: We are receiving co-operation from all levels of government as we require it. The program is going ahead well. It has not been inhibited in any way by any lack of co-operation on the part of anybody. As far as the problem of restoring the balance of fish life in the lakes is concerned I might say this. Concurrently new types of gear are being developed for the catching of smelts in the great lakes in greater volume than was possible by earlier methods.

I should like to ask the Minister of Fisheries whether his department has used any influence on the great lakes fishery commission with respect to the suggestion I have made over the past couple of years, namely to do something about stopping these lamprey from coming in from the ocean. It seems to me that we are spending a great deal of money on lampricide year after year and that nothing has been done about the source of the infestation. I suggest that some sort of electrical barrier be put somewhere on the St. Lawrence river to stop these predators from getting into the great lakes system.
[Mr. MacLean (Queens) .1

speechtext: I might say that the international great lakes fishery commission has examined all these possibilities. The problem now is, as it were, to control the predator on their front, the area to which they migrate farthest. There is such a great infestation in the lakes now that it would be locking the stable door after the steed has escaped. But this is something that is being closely watched. If we succeed in cleaning out the lakes we will, of course, have this problem raised by the hon. member for Grey North looked into.

speakeroldname: Hon. H. J. Flemming (Minister of Forestry):
speakerposition: Minister of Forestry

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the outset of my remarks, I would be remiss in failing to congratulate the minister not only on his appointment to the new Department of Forestry, but also on the presentation of his first estimates.
As the minister mentioned, I think it is useful, in analysing the policy of the new department, to refer to the recommendations of the committee on mines, forests and waters. In a report tabled in the house on July 4, 1959 the committee recommended:
Your committee strongly recommends consideration of steps which would widen the scope of the forestry branch, increasing its status in such a way that a deputy minister would be in direct charge. The fact that such a status, comparable to that of a department does not exist now reflects a lack of appreciation of the importance of the forest industries to Canada, in the past, now, and in the future. Other departments of government are considered essential to serve industries or aspects of our national economy which are of much lesser economic consequence.
Then, on page 668 of the Journals of the house, we find this recommendation:
Your committee recommends that the entomological and plant pathology research relating to trees and forests, now under the Department of Agriculture, be transferred to and co-ordinated directly with the recommended and expanded forestry department.
And now, Mr. Chairman, referring to page 669 of the report of the standing committee on mines, forests and waters, and particularly to paragraph 70, here is what we find:

Supply-Forestry
Your committee feels that Canada cannot afford to ignore a potential so great for lumber and pulp sales as is offered in the Orient and, therefore, it recommends that these markets be approached on an open-minded basis. Study should be made of our changing share of traditional markets in the U.K. and the U.S.A. A marketing section should be created within the proposed department of forestry to aid the Department of Trade and Commerce in the merchandising of our wood products.
We can say that the first recommendation has been followed, but we do not think that the mere fact of setting up the department is enough to give adequate recognition to the importance of the forestry industry.
The second suggestion has also been adopted. With regard to the third, however, the department in the past year has added absolutely nothing to what was done previously, and apparently has totally ignored the recommendation of the committee as well as the great potential markets offered in the Orient.
We are of the opinion that the department should not only co-ordinate certain activities of departments like agriculture and northern affairs and national resources, but that, in addition to research, it should set up, as suggested, a marketing service within the department.
Such a service could assist the Department of Trade and Commerce in the marketing of our wood products.
Mr. Chairman, everybody recognizes the importance of the forest industry to Canada. It could not be otherwise considering that 68 per cent of the land area of the ten provinces consists of forest land. In this regard, it must be kept in mind that this is almost four times as great as the area devoted to agriculture. Here is what the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) stated on June 28, 1960, as reported on page 5485 of Hansard:
I think I might commence by placing before the committee in summary form a few pertinent facts regarding the importance of the forest industry to Canada. More than 40 per cent of the land area of the 10 provinces consists of productive forest land. This area, by way of comparison, is almost four times as great as the area devoted to agriculture, which in capsule form reveals the extent of our forest resources. The pulp and paper industry is Canada's largest manufacturing industry; the lumber industry still stands high on the list. These industries are distributed throughout the country from coast to coast, and in addition to producing products of great value they are among the major sources of employment. External trade in wood, wood products and paper yields a balance in Canada's favour far larger than that contributed by any of the other major commodity groups

recognized in national statistics form. Furthermore, a very large proportion of that favourable balance becomes available in United States funds.
Further on, the Prime Minister had this to say:
I might point out that in September, 1959, the food and agriculture organization brought out a report dealing with paper and paper products which stated in summary form that while world demand for paper and paper products in 1955 amounted to 56 million metric tons, in 1965 it will amount to 88 million metric tons and by 1975 to 134 million metric tons.
If Canada presently supplies 16 per cent of the world market, I feel it is appropriate that we should intensify research work so as to meet the demand, but it is also very important that the forestry department ensures that we keep that market, and that is where a marketing service would be just as useful within the department as a research service.
We do not wish to minimize the importance of the pulp and paper industry, but we feel that the lumber and related industries are also quite important; yet, to our knowledge, the new department has not done much in that respect.
The department should not just administer the division it has inherited from the Department of Agriculture, that is the forest biology division, because it was not of great consequence within that department. Research in the field of forest biology should be stepped up. And the same remark applies to the former division of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
Mr. Avila Bedard, the former Quebec deputy minister of land and forests, reports that the following was written at the beginning of the eighteenth century by Intendant Dupuy:
Wood should be considered as the resource of Canada which will replace fur-trading. Wheat and wood, he added, will be the two great trading products of the country. It is therefore one resource substituted to another by Providence and there should be use and not abuse of it.
Times have changed since the eighteenth century when forests were burned by settlers clearing land. Today the emphasis is on conservation.
We know from history also that forest depletion was mainly the result of forest fires, insects and fungi, as well as of the normal action of nature's forces.
Nowadays, thanks to scientific developments, such plagues can be curbed.
Mr. Bedard also reports that in 1886 a German, Otto Hann, foresaw all the possibilities. He wrote:

It occurs to me that Canada will know how to make use of its vast forest resources for making paper to satisfy not only its continental, but also its international needs.
We have since covered a good deal of ground to arrive at a radical change. Things have changed greatly from the economic point of view since the beginning of the colony. How right was the man who wrote that, for our country has now become the first exporter of this commodity.
The paper industry ranks first among our great manufacturing industries.
The two earliest censuses, those of 185051 and of 1860-61, indicate that there were then five or six paper mills in the province of Quebec.
Both parts of Canada had at that time 16 paper mills whose production had a value of $372,000.
The Canada Year Book reveals that, in 1957, our exports reached $715,490,000, and it is expected our production should double within about 15 years.
Lumber and other forest products are also of great importance in that industry.
Mr. Marie Albert Bourget, in a book entitled La Foret, one of a collection on our environment, points out that local needs, as well as the needs, even limited, of the mother country, could not but make for the early establishment of saw mills.
And he mentions that as early as 1668, Mr. Hazeur established two saw mills at La Mal-baie and that about 50 years later, in 1720, the country had about 28 such mills and that in 1732, 10 new constructions showed that it was possible to find a source of wealth there.
Here again, we have come a long way: the figures for 1957 show that the export value of boards and beams amounted to $281,681,000.
From an economic point of view, forest products continue to make a most important contribution toward a reduction of our trade deficits.
On the domestic level, the forest industry paid salaries and wages amounting to $1,117 million in 1958.
The same year, forest operations gave jobs to 67,327 people, and those figures have been compiled on a man-year basis and exclude men engaged in transportation activities.
If we consider that the pulp and paper industry gave employment to 64,084 people, the lumber industry to 47,763, the wood products industry to 73,159, and the paper products industry to 28,851, we can appreciate the economic contribution of that important market.
90205-6-389J
Supply-Forestry
That source of employment and wealth we have in our forests has a great social value for our country.
Our forest resources must be used to meet the needs of our population, and with its welfare in mind and it is up to this new department to co-operate closely with the provinces and the various research and conservation organizations, so as to set up an economic and social policy and search for the most efficient formulas to reach that end.
The solution depends in the first place on the kind of resources to be developed.
Now, here in this country, there are no problems as far as that is concerned, providing there is reforestation and intelligent development.
From the point of view of conservation and reforestation, we have in Canada an organization concerned with action in the field of forestry and whose objective it is to obtain public co-operation in the wise use of our renewable resources.
I am thinking of the Canadian Forestry Association, which was founded about the year 1900, under the patronage of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, and which organized the first conference on conservation.
In 1959, it became a federation of provincial forestry associations. It has to its credit the organization of three national conferences on resources, in 1906, 1954 and 1958.
That organization comprises the following groups throughout Canada: Canadian Forestry Association of B.C.; L'Association Forestiere du Quebec with its ten regional groups; Ontario Forestry Association; Manitoba Forestry Association; Alberta Forestry Association; Saskatchewan Forestry Association; Canadian Forestry Association of New Brunswick; Canadian Forestry Association of Nova Scotia.
The association has a membership of 35,000 adults and 18,500 young people. Since their registration, the junior forest wardens have brought in 39,500 boys and the Quebec 4-H clubs 56,000 boys and girls.
These youth organizations have many activities, including fire warden clubs, summer camps, annual contests, forestry schools, conservation, etc.
Among the public at large, the association has been a great protector of the forest through its educational activities, using various media such as the press, radio broadcasts, movies and the distribution of literature.
In addition, forest fire prevention campaigns are organized each year.
Since 1954, tree farms have been included in the program, and so far, the association had to its credit, as of December 31, 1960,

Supply-Forestry
820 such farms with a total area of 515,000 privately owned acres.
To this well-rounded program, the Canadian Forestry Association has added studies on sylviculture and reforestation.
This is a very brief summary of the work done by the federation of provincial forestry associations, whose sole purpose is to educate the people on the problems of forestry, which it considers as crucial.
We now have in Ottawa a forestry department. It was set up with a great flourish of publicity, but perhaps it is important to raise the matter of the co-operation it can offer to the members of the federation, to find out whether it is just a ghost department or whether it really intends to do something worthwhile.
In March of this year, a brief was submitted to the minister, specifically requesting an increase in the $20,000 subsidy now being granted by the department.
When you look at the efforts put forth and the results obtained by the federation, it seems to me that this request for $100,000 was reasonable. However, it apparently did not get the consideration it deserved from the new department or indeed from the minister who, I must admit, has great experience in this field. It is not that the federation did not have a good case, but the government seems hard to convince. I would not like to accuse the minister of refusing to raise this subsidy because he saw no political advantage in such a course, though I must say this is a specialty of the government.
However, here are the arguments put forward when this brief was submitted, and I think they are most realistic and convincing. It is stated in the first place, and I quote:
(Text):
1.	Investing in the associations is much cheaper for the government than trying to do his job itself.
2.	The job of conservation education we are doing is a "long term preventive unemployment medicine", as Canada's future hangs on the wise use of resources.
3.	C.F.A. can tell the public about the activities and the importance of the Department of Forestry in a way this latter could not; so, the value of C.F.A. for the public relations of the Department of Forestry could be very high.
4.	The Department of Forestry Act states that public education is a right and proper field for the new department to engage in.
5.	The expansion of the access roads in the forest requires parallel education of travelling public.
6.	Forest protection against fire starts with prevention and prevention is a matter of information and education.

7.	Boy scouts are receiving an annual grant from the federal government; so are the agricultural youth clubs. Forestry youth clubs, which are- not to say more-as active as the others, have never been helped.
8.	All meetings dealing with natural resources and forestry, and it will certainly be the same with the resources for tomorrow conference, recommend more public information and education regarding the conservation of the forests; it is exactly the work of C.F.A.
9.	By providing a nationally integrated conservation program, the federation of provincial forestry associations presents a ready-forged medium of communication which, we feel, deserves the fullest support from government at all levels.
(Translation) :
It seems to me that the arguments put forward were rather convincing, but the minister took no heed of them to date.
It is indeed to the credit of the government to have set up this department, but, up to now, it has accomplished nothing more than was done before by the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources.
The Canadian Forestry Association pointed out to the minister that its request was based on clause VI of Bill C-82 of the Forestry Department Act, and stated moreover, that it had the support of all ministers of lands and forests in the eight provinces which have forestry associations.
Moreover, the provinces were willing to remit the amount due to each association, through their departments of lands and forests, or directly through the national federation.
In the case of the required amount, which was $100,000-of which $25,000 were for the federation itself, while the balance was equal to the amount now subscribed by provincial governments for their provincial forestry associations-the federal government would only have contributed on a 50-50 basis in that field, as it does in many others.
We know that the present federal grant to the federation is $20,000. Of course, with the creation of the new forestry department the federation expected a more generous contribution from the federal government for such important education work with regard to our natural and forest resources. It was an excellent opportunity for the new minister, when speaking, on March 10, at the annual assembly, to show that his department had not been set up solely in order to give a post to a former premier who had been defeated in his own province but who had moreover, as a Conservative feather in his cap, the advantage of having moved the choice of the present Prime Minister rather than the Minister of Finance or the Minister of Justice at the Conservative convention in Ottawa.

This department, like all others, seems to have fallen asleep and to care but little about what is happening.
I do not want to be unfair to the minister who has the personal ability to do much more and the necessary knowledge to do well in his department, which, however, seems to have been steeped in the same uneasiness as all departments under this government.
This niggardly refusal to accede to the request of the only Canadian association concerned with forest conservation in Canada is an additional proof of this government's anarchy.
As I said, the minister has all my admiration.

Will the hon. member permit a question? In his summation of the request of the Canadian Forestry Association, will he make quite clear the contribution now being made by the provinces which, incidentally, are the only recipients of revenue from this natural resource while at the same time they contribute only 15 per cent of the total amount required to run this association?
