Mr. Chairman, I have no intention of discussing the contributions made by each of Canada's ten provinces.
I am sure that my hon. friend is more interested in what the government of British Columbia is doing in this respect. It may be that that province contributes only 15 per cent.
As I was saying, I personally trust the minister. However one thing I should like to say is that the Prime Minister should consider him as qualified as we do on this side of the house, and that he should not be used any more as a mere messenger between Ottawa and New Brunswick, and as a propagandist for the government.
This department was organized with a view to co-ordinating research work to promote production and forest resources conservation in Canada; unfortunately, we find that nothing has been done to that effect, that all that used to be done previously-and not only would it be advisable but it would even be more important that the government should do away with the routine followed by certain sectors of the departments of northern affairs and of agriculture, and that a real desire to look after our forests be shown.
In addition to marketing, as I said in my opening remarks and as the committee suggested, the department should be aware that
Supply-Forestry
it can do much more. It should be recognized that the training of people in forestry should be positive and well controlled. Methods should vary as between cities and rural areas, and as between lumbermen and industry.
We on this side of the house are often accused of criticizing and not making any suggestions. By contrast to that and as we usually do, I should like to draw the minister's attention to certain suggestions which could be given greater consideration by his department. Most of the suggestions I wish to make could be considered and applied in co-operation with the provinces, because I am one of many who still believe that the rights of the provinces concerning forestry must come first.
Everyone knows that the provinces own almost all of our forest resources in Canada, and so they must remain the only administrators of those riches. It is with pleasure that I heard the minister restate that policy again today. However, what I have to suggest could be realized on the basis of cooperation as in the case of access roads because never, never, and on that I perfectly agree with the minister, should this department open the door to interference with purely provincial matters.
I feel that there is nothing wrong with the promotion of continued co-operation between federal and provincial governments and a recent Ottawa meeting of the ministers of forestry of Ontario, New Brunswick and Quebec shows that they are ready to cooperate. The minister himself having given us an indication to that effect, I believe that we have there proof of a real desire to co-operate without the slightest infringement upon the rights of the provinces.
Here are a few suggestions which the Department of Forestry might consider and thus help all the provinces.
First of all, it could help increase real model forests across the country like they have in the United States.
Second, it could co-operate with experimental farms where there is already a wood lot in order that it be developed and used as an outdoor laboratory. I refer especially to the Lennoxville experimental farm near Sherbrooke.
Third, it should increase research on the use of our hard woods.
Fourth, it should increase research on the use of our soft woods.
I was very pleased indeed this week to receive a pamphlet from the Department of Forestry, entitled "Properties and utilization

Supply-Forestry
of Canadian poplars". I might tell you, Mr. Chairman, that it is a most interesting pamphlet and I wish to commend the officials who prepared it. If I may be allowed to express a wish-may it be distributed all over Canada and also be sent to different manufacturers.
Fifth, the department could increase its grants to forestry associations, as requested by the Canadian Forestry Association.
Sixth, the department could give more help in order to promote reforestation of waste lands. A bill along this line has been introduced in the house by the Minister of Agriculture. I wonder why this question of reforestation has not been left to the Department of Forestry instead of being handled by the Department of Agriculture.
Seventh, the department could help in setting up and maintaining nurseries.
Eighth, the department could set up an exhibition of forestry products from every province, and send it all over Canada and abroad. On this point, I should like to quote the following article which was published in the 1961 issue of the magazine entitled Timber:
(Text):
Early in January, 1962, while Canada slumbers under a blanket of snow, a Canadian "army" will move eastward to West Africa, where snow and frost are unknown to most of the inhabitants. Although sponsored by the Canadian government, this army will go in peace. The soldiers are Canadian manufacturers and merchants, their ammunition consisting of nothing other than a briefcase containing advertising material describing the products they wish to sell. Their aim is to sell the Africans only such goods as will foster their development and aid their economic progress.
(Translation):
The department should bear the cost of the exhibition and organize an increasingly greater number of events in different countries, in order to promote and expand our exports of forest products. Our domestic trade should also be promoted by familiarizing Canadians with products made in Canada.
It could also-and this is my ninth suggestion-patronize a special fire prevention week each year in co-operation with the provinces.
Tenth, it could also immediately increase grants to the provinces, so that the forestry inventory can be drawn up as soon as possible. Knowing exactly what the resources and the industrial potential of our forests are, the opportunities in both fields could be determined. I know that the Department of Forestry

is co-operating in the inventory of provincial forests, and I wonder if it would not be appropriate to increase these grants.
Eleventh, it could promote reforestation and development by setting up long term forestry credit facilities. I believe that this suggestion is by far the most important, for it would prompt many farmers operating on marginal lands to undertake reforestation and the development on those lands.
Twelfth, the department should study the qualities of some varieties of trees which are not being used at present, so as to give the industries now using hardwood a chance of maintaining their operations with varieties which have been left aside, for it appears that hardwood lots are being depleted.
Many other suggestions could be made, but I believe it would be a step forward if the department would take under immediate consideration those I have just mentioned.
However, as I say, in order not to be misunderstood, these steps should be applied so as not to encroach upon the rights of the provinces who have exclusive jurisdiction in the administration of their own forests. I see that the minister is smiling; he understands why I stress co-operation between his department and the provinces. He knows I want no interference in provincial jurisdiction. If it has been possible to co-operate in the access roads program, then I believe a similar procedure could be followed to apply the recommendations I have just made.
In the May 1961 issue of the magazine Timber, reference is made to a speech given by the Minister of Forestry on the occasion of the sixtieth anniversary of the Canadian Forestry Association. I should like to quote part of the article which is entitled:
(Text):
Flemming addresses C.F.A. annual meeting.

(Text):
1.	Continue and increase the current programs of research relating to forestry and the utilization of forest products.
2.	Maintain and increase the information branch of the forestry department.
3.	Provide economic studies of forest resources and forest industries.
4.	Aid provincial agencies, or individuals, in specific forestry programs.
5.	Provide forest surveys, technical advice and other assistance to any federal agency dealing with forest lands.
6.	Co-operate with international organizations (such as U.N. agencies) concerned with forestry, and in which Canada has membership.

Mr. Chairman, I thank the committee for its patience and I will try to conclude as briefly as possible.
As I was saying, it is strange indeed to come so often across the words "continue" and "maintain". The forestry department has not been set up, I believe, solely to maintain without any change what already existed in the Departments of Agriculture and Northern Affairs and National Resources, because we should then be justified in saying that if that were the intention of the minister -I do not think it was-the new department was unnecessary.
The booklet entitled "Canadian Forestry Statistics", and more particularly table 16 on page 18, provides the following indications. I quote the figures on exports of wood products.

The average for the three years from 1954 to 1956 inclusive is $347 million, while that for the years 1957 to 1959 inclusive is $300 million, that is, an annual decrease of $47 million. That is why I believe the setting up of a sales service in the department is most important.
The forest industry itself is doing everything possible. The magazine also pointed out the various continuing steps taken by industry in this regard, and I quote the article:
(Text):
New Canadian hardwood grade for the U.K. market Strenuous efforts are being made to boost shipments of Canadian hardwoods to Britain this year
Supply-Forestry
and to build up a larger future trade more comparable with pre-war business. First shots in this campaign were fired last year when the Canadian lumber trade mission visited the U.K., and now there has been a follow-up by a visit from two hardwood specialists-Mr. Robert Staniforth, director and general manager of Staniforth Lumber and Veneer, Ltd., and a director of the C.L.A.; and Mr. Jack Barrier, chief inspector for the N.H.L.A.
They have made a brief springtime visit to Britain with the aim of selling the U.K. trade on a new utility grade of Canadian hardwoods for the furniture and pallet industries at economic prices. The Canadian shipment of 750,000 cu. ft. of hardwoods last year to Britain is not enough- they- want to get back to the figure of 1940- 6,600,000 cu. ft.
(Translation):
Mr. Chairman, I am wondering whether we should not see there another indication of the usefulness and the contribution of the Department of Forestry particularly through support to our trade commissioners promoting a Canadian product everywhere in the world. It seems to me that the statistics are selfexplanatory and that they show the urgency of the problem.
As for the situation of supply, I quote page 203 of the report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects. It reads:
Does Canada possess the forests capable of meeting the projected increases in output of wood products? The requirements of wood to meet the various projected productions of forest products have been estimated for us.
Based on these estimates, to meet the 1980 requirements of the wood-using industries, the annual cut of wood will have to be 58 per cent larger than it was in 1954. These estimates include sizeable allowance for increased use of mill leftovers-waste material-in the production of pulp and paper. We are told that at the projected level of lumber, plywood and veneer output, as much as 6 million to 8 million cords of usable material would result as waste.
Mr. Chairman, I feel that the supply situation must be correlated with the possibilities of sales and exports, if stability is to be maintained in that most important industry. To verify that point let us refer once again to the report on Canada's economic prospects, particularly page 193 in connection with only one section of that industry. I quote:
We shall begin with the lumber or saw mill industry, one of Canada's oldest manufacturing operations but still one of its largest. In output, sawmilling still ranks within the leading ten manufacturing industries; in employment it rivals the pulp and paper industry. It is an industry made up of more than 8,000 mills, many of which are very small, but some of which are extremely large.
Research within the department must not only be maintained but accelerated, and the central government, through this new department, should accelerate research and offer its co-operation to the provinces, while respecting their sovereign rights, in order that an inventory be made and that the development of our forests and protection against

Supply-Forestry
forest fires, insect, cryptogamic disease be carried out; that reforestation methods to increase output be discovered; that better utilization of forest products be achieved and that a study of market requirements be made to find ways of selling the products; that the system of forest concessions which is too uncertain at present and therefore paralyses the progress of forestry be stabilized; that the financial structure of our industry be adjusted; that research be made into forest economics, technology and science; and finally that higher specialized education in forestry be developed to give the government the administrators it needs, and to provide industry with good technicians to help it maintain its position.
I would not want my remarks to be misinterpreted; neither would I want to minimize the work carried out by departmental officials. But I condemn the government for its lack of action. It seems to me that since it was established, the department has not accomplished what the forest industry had the right to expect.
I have here a pamphlet issued by the laboratories of Canadian forest products entitled:
(Text):
Comparison of taper sawing and through-and-through sawing.
(Translation):
This document is most interesting and important for every saw mill in our country and it is well made, because it might help small saw mills which cannot afford to retain the services of experts. I should like the department to tell us how many of those pamphlets were distributed and whether they are available in both official languages.
On the other hand, I have here three other pamphlets published by the laboratory. The first one is entitled;
(Text):
Some effects of Mill type on the sawing of small logs.
(Translation):
The second one is called:

Strengthening ring-connectored timbers with steel strapping.
(Translation):
And the third one:

Wear, play and heat distortion in veneer lathes.
(Translation) :
Those pamphlets are most interesting and the department is to be commended for having re-issued them. I hope they were distributed in all provinces.

I hope the Prime Minister will have as much confidence in the Minister of Forestry as we have, and that he will provide him and his officials, whom I want to congratulate, with the means to accomplish things that will show that the head of the government had good grounds for creating the new department, which has not been proved so far.
Private enterprise deserves also our congratulations, as well as the different forestry organizations for their unfailing co-operation.
Briefly, I want not only to congratulate the minister for what he has done in the past, but to ask him to do much more in the future.
Moreover, I trust that all the hopes raised by his appointment will be fulfilled, and that those who have entertained such hopes will soon have clear evidence of the capital importance he wants to give to the question of our forests.

Mr. Chairman, the hon.
member is inaccurate in his statement. I threw out the suggestion the other night that on Thursday between five and six o'clock, or alternatively on Friday between five and six o'clock, we might deal with private and public bills.
On Saturday.

speechtext: It was not agreed to by all parties. The second suggestion that I threw out was that if we finished justice, fisheries and forestry early today, I would be quite prepared to move the adjournment of the house. I thought perhaps hon. members would finish by 4.30. However, that has not happened, so we are continuing.
That is right.
Mr. Chairman, I have had so many phone calls lately and committee meetings-
And letters.
-and correspondence-
Yes.
-and visitors-
Yes.

-that I have had very little time to do much reading or get together a few notes in anticipation of the estimates of this important department. However, I do want to say that the members of this group, naturally, having urged the necessity and the need for a Department of Forestry for many years, are very pleased that this department has been formed. In forming this department the government has recognized the importance of the management of our forests, the needs of the industry so far as the department is concerned and, on that account, the necessity for a department whose sole responsibility is to devote its attention to these matters.
Before proceeding I wish to compliment the minister on his appointment as the first Minister of Forestry for Canada. I wish him every success in all he undertakes with respect to the activities of his department. I think it will provide a great opportunity for plenty of work because there are a great many things which require to be done and which have not been done in the past. The minister will have an opportunity to do these things because of the establishment of this department, provided, Mr. Chairman, that in the years to come we see the estimate for the Department of Forestry is considerably greater than $15,464,427. I do not think it would be fair, possibly, on the first estimates of this department to expect too much, but when we consider the importance of the forest industry to the economy of Canada I think it is quite right for hon. members of this house to expect to see that importance recognized in the years ahead by a greatly increased estimate for this department.
Mr. Chairman, as I said before, I am going to speak quite briefly on this subject. The forests of our country, their management and the forest industry are very seriously affected by the policies of both federal and provincial governments. It is one of those spheres where there is a great deal of overlapping in a number of aspects. Therefore the first essential, if this department is going to be a success and if the management of our forests is going to be along the proper lines and our industry is going to prosper, is that there should be co-operation between federal and provincial governments to this end. I do urge that every effort be made 90205-6-390
Supp ly-F orestry
on the part of the minister to promote this co-operation, particularly in view of the opportunities provided him as minister of this new department.
I think a second essential is a national policy for the conservation, development and utilization of our renewable natural resources, of which the forest resources are a very major portion. I trust that as a result of the resources for tomorrow conference we will see a step forward in that direction. For years we have urged as a second necessity the need for a national policy to this end. If the department has the funds, if we have the required federal-provincial co-operation, and if we have agreement on principles and policies with respect to the conservation, utilization and development of our natural resources, we are on the right road to steer a steady and permanent course for the greater development of this industry.
I listened with interest to the minister's speech, which naturally on this occasion dealt with the organization of his department. I was glad the minister informed the committee of this organization and certain aspects of it. The minister told us that the heads of branches in this department are, as we anticipated, experienced personnel who have had service in this field. The minister also said that the recruits to the department would be obtained through civil service examinations, and so on.
Then the minister mentioned a matter that is interesting to me. I refer to the co-ordination within the department, particularly with regard to the various branches that have to do with forest management, forest development, forest research, forest products research and research into diseases, pests, and so on. The minister then mentioned his plans for co-ordination with other departments, particularly, I presume, with the Department of Agriculture and the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys. He then mentioned it is the intention of his department to cooperate with various international organizations which are concerned with the international aspects of the development of the forest industry. I think that is a very important segment of the department's activities which can be developed to a greater extent in the years ahead. It is very closely related to the scientific development and utilization of forest products and also to our marketing abroad.
I was interested recently to read an article in Saturday Night. The only reading I do is usually in bed after eleven o'clock in order to try to get some sleep when I have been particularly annoyed by a speech made by someone on the benches opposite. This is an interesting article and very thoughtfully

Supply-Forestry
written by Mr. Robson Black. It expresses a changed relationship between the forest industry and the rest of our economy as well as a changing situation inside the industry itself. The article appeared in the issue of April 2, and it reads in part:
The fortune-tellers who once spelled out Canada's destiny appraised the nation's timberlands as a diminishing and expendable asset in the balance sheets of the future. They did not foresee that a perishable resource can do something better than to perish; it can add and multiply.
That shift in emphasis only occurred because of the change which has come about in the attitude to our forest resources taken by governments and, fortunately, in recent years by industry itself. The writer goes on to say:
The most dramatic proof that Canada has emerged from forest exploitation to "resource management" is the decision of the pulp and paper industry to double production by 1980.
That would have been unheard of 20 years ago.
Such doubling entails an extraction of an additional 15 million cords of wood annually, more than twice as much as is now required. To attain that level of raw material will impose a systematic harvesting of the increment of the tree growth without impairing the total "capital stock". This may seem a curious sequel to early tales of Canadian saw mills "pursuing" the forest from township to township in an ever-widening swath of spoliation. Unfortunately it is from such storied accounts that so many Canadians rate their woodlands as a fugitive possession.
Unfortunately there are many people who still have that conception and who have not realized that a change in direction has taken place. I remember as a boy seeing timber thoughtlessly destroyed, though on a much smaller scale than has happened in the history of eastern Canada. But the assurance that our forests will be managed throughout the years is to be found in a statement such as I have read indicating that planning is taking place for tremendously increased production, because this is where self-interest will guide the activities of these companies engaged in the industry. The tremendous and increasing investment in the industry in plant and equipment will make the wise management of our forests necessary as a means of protecting the investment itself, otherwise the investment would not be made. The article goes on to say:
No other industry is so suited to Canada's natural advantages of great forests, abundant water and power supplies, in the utilization of which pulp and paper manufacture has made its own way without subsidies, price floors, guarantees or other forms of public assistance.
I think that is to the credit of the lumber industry, the pulp and paper industry and all segments of the forest industry. Then I read, further, in this article on the subject of the general situation in the forest industry and the pulp and paper industry:

Legislation and tax structures now encircling forest industry offer little encouragement to those seeking to practice constructive management on their timberlands.
I can assure hon. members that I have personal knowledge of this. I could speak with great feeling on this question.
They effectively erase whatever rewards an operator might expect from paying conservation costs on a public-owned estate. New forest regulations must be drafted, the tenure of licensed woodlands made secure and, in general, the long-outmoded concepts of government partnership with forest industry will have to be re-stated in enlightened terms. Lacking a prompt and liberal re-orientation on the part of the government landlord, the industrial tenant will be in no position to contribute his full quota to national advancement.
That was written, particularly, I think with respect to the type of timber management leases in operation in Ontario and, on a larger scale, in British Columbia. But even those who own their land and timber are suffering from the same disability and this is something to which both federal and provincial governments should give a great deal of attention.
The pulp and paper Industry also faces a hazard of federal political policy that may constrict its competitive position in world trade.
The first hazard is related to uncoordinated and unscientific taxation policies. The next has to do with political policy which may constrict Canada's competitive position in world trade. The writer asks:
To what degree should Canada's economic program be shaped by the needs of her primary natural resources industries? Should protective tariffs and other restraints on imports seek to proliferate secondary enterprises, thereby raising production costs for the export industries and reducing the power of foreign markets to buy Canadian products?
I think there is a good thought there. While we want to promote the development of secondary industry, if we do so by means of protective policies and things of that sort we shall be affecting the greatest sources of our revenue, which are the lands, forests and mines of this country. The writer goes on to refer to Swedish public policy-and there is a lot to be learned from Sweden both in regard to government economics and forest management. He says:
Swedish public policy and advanced technical skills have succeeded in keeping the country's timberlands matched to the needs of 190 pulp or paper mills and 4,000 saw mills. Quite true, secondary industries also have multiplied and greatly prospered but without artificial stimulation. The Swedish government has adhered to a tariff protection scale never higher than 9 per cent, the lowest in the world except for Denmark. The national policy of minimum tariffs is. in effect, an ultimatum to secondary industry to "keep on its toes ", to compete for domestic and export trade through maximum technical efficiency in manufacturing processes and vigorous pursuit of home and foreign buyers.

In conclusion, this writer says:
It is well to decide what Canadian product is most durably founded upon an ascending international demand and is best prepared to bring increase and enrichment to the Canadian people and new security to the nation's most vital natural resource. We must turn to our pulp and paper industry for the answer.
And also, I would say, we must turn to the other basic primary industries of this country upon which we depend so much for our prosperity. The minister dealt with a number of other questions. I wish to emphasize before concluding that I believe there is great scope for increased and improved public relations as one of the functions of the department in order that the Canadian people may better understand what this forest heritage means to them as far as prosperity, economic development and recreation are concerned.
I believe special consideration should be given to the taxation policies of both federal and provincial governments. Do you know, Mr. Chairman, the policies in this respect both federal and provincial are hit and miss in this regard? The large companies in Canada engaged in the forest industry get exemptions in respect of investments in road developments and other developments but the smaller operators do not enjoy the same advantages because of certain technicalities in the Income Tax Act. This is something which the minister will be well advised to consider, namely the position of the small operator under that act as compared with the position of the large operator. In some cases, of course, small operators lose advantages because of ignorance of the provisions and lack of advice from appropriate persons. In British Columbia, at the present time, the government of that province is actually taxing the owner of private land on his capital in standing timber. Not only does he pay land tax and a royalty when his timber is cut but he must pay a tax on his standing timber, too. That is just the same as taxing a man on his capital in the bank, or his capital invested in bonds, or on any other personal asset, rather than taxing him on the revenue, the interest, the income or the profit.
The last item I wish to mention, which I think is of tremendous importance, is the research which is required in respect of marketing. There are new opportunities opening up through the changing of conditions throughout the world. We in British Columbia believe that Asia is going to be one of the great markets in the future for the forest industry of British Columbia. I suggest that this department, in addition to its research into forest management, the protection of 90205-6-3904
Supply-Forestry
forests from insects and fire, forestry inventory activities, and the roads to resources program, as well as the very necessary research into forest products, should undertake a program of research in respect to marketing possibilities in addition to that which now takes place through the Department of Trade and Commerce.
Mr. Chairman, I have spoken quite briefly in discussing the few items which came to my mind as I sat here. Once again I should like to say to the minister, as one who has spent most of his life among trees, sawdust and horses, that I wish him well in all he undertakes in the management of this department, and look forward in the years ahead to a much larger appropriation and a great extension in his activities.

Mr. Chairman, perhaps the committee will indulge me for a few moments during which time I wish to speak in regard to the estimates of the Department of Forestry. I should first of all like to congratulate the minister on his appointment as the first minister of the Department of Forestry, and suggest that he has a mighty big job on his hands to some extent occasioned by a difficulty in respect to federal-provincial co-operation.
We have heard a great deal this afternoon from the hon. member for Beauce about provincial rights. I suggest to him that, first and foremost, each time a province accepts a right it must also accept a responsibility. My remarks this afternoon will have reference to that subject.
In Alberta at this moment the forest areas are suffering from the most serious forest fire situation which has existed for some time. There are over 105,000 acres of forest land either burning, or burnt off. There have been 367 fires in the Edson area alone, with 30,000 acres of forest land burnt off or now burning. This is a very serious situation. I asked the Minister of National Defence on Tuesday last whether he had received a request for the assistance of the armed service. His reply was that he had not received such a request. I suggest this is the type of problem in regard to which there must exist federal-provincial co-operation. It appears that because of an unnatural pride on the part of some in regard to provincial rights the people of northwestern Alberta are facing a serious handicap which they should not have to face. At this moment, in all the towns of that area other industries are suffering serious hardships because of the fact that all available manpower is out on the fire lines. It seems reasonable to me to suggest that a co-ordinating council at

Supply-Forestry
the federal level should be established to coordinate fire fighting activities in all provinces of Canada, so as to make available all the firefighting equipment possible, and to establish a system to facilitate the successful use of air force and army personnel to fight these very serious outbreaks of fires which are now taking place.
I should like to point out that there appears to be some delay particularly in respect of Alberta in making requests for help. This might well be the result of political reasoning more than because individuals do not wish more to be done in regard to this serious situation.
Before I conclude, Mr. Chairman, I should like again to make the suggestion I made to the minister shortly after his appointment. The forestry laboratories located at Kan-anaskis should be moved to the centre of the forest industry in Alberta, which I suggest is the Hinton-Edson area. I make this suggestion to him again because I feel that the centre of the timber industry in Alberta, being in that area, would lend itself to closer cooperation between the department's research facilities and the commercial operators so that the gap which it is felt has developed, between the research done by the department and the research it is felt should be done, might be lessened or perhaps eliminated.
I feel that the amount of money which the federal government is paying on a shared basis with the provinces, particularly in regard to forest inventories, reforestation and forest protection, should be considered seriously with a view to making sure that the
provinces not only accept their rights but accept their responsibilities.

Mr. Chairman, may I call it six o'clock.
